text: In January 1077 Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow for three days outside a fortress in northern Italy to seek forgiveness. Pope Gregory VII had excommunicated him during a dispute over who could appoint bishops. The fortress belonged to Matilda of Tuscany. For 10 points, name this castle whose name is a byword for submission to authority.

This 1204 crusade, supported by Venice under Doge Enrico Dandolo, never reached Egypt or the Holy Land. Instead its army sacked the capital of the Byzantine Empire. A Latin Empire was set up afterward. For 10 points, name this crusade numbered fourth.

From 1309 to 1377 the popes lived in this city in southern France instead of Rome. Clement V began the practice. The period was followed by the Western Schism. For 10 points, name this city, whose papal palace still stands.

This English dynastic conflict between the houses of Lancaster and York began in 1455. Richard III was killed at Bosworth Field in 1485, and Henry Tudor took the throne. For 10 points, name this series of civil wars named for flowers.

This Bohemian reformer and rector of Charles University was burned at the stake at the Council of Constance in 1415. His followers, the Hussites, fought crusades against them. He was inspired by John Wycliffe. For 10 points, name this man.

This Habsburg ruler was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain as Charles I. He presided over the Diet of Worms and abdicated in 1556, dividing his lands between his son and brother. For 10 points, name this ruler, numbered five.

In August 1572 Catholic mobs in Paris killed thousands of Huguenots after the wedding of Henry of Navarre to Margaret of Valois. Catherine de Medici is often blamed. The massacre is named for the feast day on which it began. For 10 points, name this massacre.

This nobleman, called "the Silent," led the Dutch Revolt against Spain's Philip II. He was a Prince of Orange and was assassinated in Delft in 1584. For 10 points, name this man, the great-grandfather of the later English king.

In 1571 a Holy League fleet defeated Ottoman forces in this naval battle in the Gulf of Patras. Don John of Austria commanded the Christian ships, and Miguel de Cervantes was wounded. For 10 points, name this battle.

This series of treaties of 1713 and 1714 ended the War of the Spanish Succession. Philip V kept the Spanish throne but renounced the French one. Britain gained Gibraltar and Minorca. For 10 points, name these treaties named for a Dutch city.

Frederick the Great of Prussia survived this global conflict of 1756 to 1763, known in America as the French and Indian War. The Treaty of Paris ended it, and Britain gained Canada. For 10 points, name this war named for its length.

In 1772, 1793, and 1795 Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided this country, which disappeared from the map until 1918. Tadeusz Kosciuszko led a failed uprising in 1794. For 10 points, name this country.

Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert edited this Enlightenment work, published from 1751 to 1772 in many volumes. It aimed to gather all knowledge and was opposed by the Church. For 10 points, name this French reference work.

In June 1789 the National Assembly's deputies met on an indoor court in Versailles and swore not to disband until they had written a constitution. Jacques-Louis David sketched it. For 10 points, name this oath.

On November 9, 1799, Napoleon Bonaparte and Emmanuel Sieyes overthrew the Directory in this coup. The date is by the revolutionary calendar. For 10 points, name this coup named for a month, which began the Consulate.

Horatio Nelson was killed at this 1805 naval battle off the coast of Spain. The British victory over a French and Spanish fleet ended Napoleon's invasion hopes. For 10 points, name this battle named for a cape.
In August 1819 cavalry charged a peaceful crowd demanding parliamentary reform in Manchester, killing about fifteen. The name mocks Waterloo. For 10 points, name this massacre at Saint Peter's Field.

This 1832 act in Britain eliminated rotten boroughs and gave seats to growing industrial cities like Manchester. Earl Grey was prime minister. For 10 points, name this first major electoral law of its kind in the nineteenth century.
This 1846 repeal of tariffs on imported grain was achieved by Robert Peel with help from Whigs and Richard Cobden. It split the Conservative Party. For 10 points, name this British legislation.

In May 1848 delegates met in Saint Paul's Church in this city to draft a constitution for a united Germany. They offered the crown to Frederick William IV of Prussia, who refused. For 10 points, name this assembly named for a city.
In 1894 a Jewish French army captain was falsely convicted of treason and sent to Devil's Island. Emile Zola wrote "J'Accuse" to defend him. For 10 points, name this scandal named for the captain.
This radical government ruled Paris in the spring of 1871 after France's defeat by Prussia. It was crushed in the "Bloody Week" by troops from Versailles. For 10 points, name this government.

The Schlieffen Plan called for Germany to defeat France quickly by marching through this neutral country. Its invasion in 1914 brought Britain into World War I. For 10 points, name this small country whose capital is Brussels.
From February to December 1916 the French and Germans fought this longest battle of World War I, around a fortress on the Meuse. Philippe Petain became a hero there. For 10 points, name this battle.
In 1923 Adolf Hitler and the Nazis tried to seize power in Munich by marching from a beer hall. The attempt failed and he was jailed. For 10 points, name this unsuccessful uprising.

Pablo Picasso painted this huge black-and-white canvas in 1937 for the Spanish Republic's pavilion at the Paris World Exposition. It shows screaming figures, a bull, and a wounded horse. It responds to the German bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. For 10 points, name this painting.
In August 1939 Germany and the USSR signed this treaty, which contained a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe. It was named for two foreign ministers. For 10 points, name this pact.

In late May and early June 1940 hundreds of small civilian boats helped rescue over 300,000 British and French soldiers from a beach and harbor in northern France. German forces had trapped the army against the sea. Winston Churchill said that wars are not won by evacuations. For 10 points, name this evacuation.
In February 1945 Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin met at this Crimean resort to plan the postwar order. They agreed to divide Germany into occupation zones. For 10 points, name this conference.

In 1968 Alexander Dubcek introduced "socialism with a human face" in this country, but Warsaw Pact troops invaded in August. For 10 points, name this country and this reform period, called a "spring" in its capital.
This Polish electrician led the Solidarity movement at the Gdansk shipyard in 1980. He won the 1983 Nobel Peace Prize and became Poland's president in 1990. For 10 points, name this man.

text: Around 1200 BC groups known by this collective name, mentioned in Egyptian inscriptions at Medinet Habu, attacked the eastern Mediterranean. Ramses III repelled them. Their migrations coincided with the collapse of Ugarit and the Hittite Empire. For 10 points, name these raiders, whose label does not describe them as a single nation.

This Assyrian king assembled a library of clay tablets at Nineveh in the seventh century BC. It preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh. He fought a civil war against his brother in Babylon. For 10 points, name this last great king of Assyria.

This Lydian king, known for his wealth, was defeated by Cyrus the Great around 546 BC. He asked the oracle at Delphi whether he should attack Persia and was told a great empire would fall. For 10 points, name this man, whose name is a byword for wealth.

In 479 BC the Greek allies under the Spartan regent Pausanias crushed the last major Persian army on Greek soil at this battle in Boeotia. The Persian commander Mardonius died. For 10 points, name this land battle.
This Athenian reformer of 594 BC canceled debts, ended debt slavery, and divided citizens into four property classes. He is counted among the Seven Sages. For 10 points, name this lawgiver.

In 371 BC this Theban general broke Sparta's reputation for invincibility at Leuctra using an oblique formation. He also freed the Messenian helots. He died at Mantinea in 362. For 10 points, name this man.

In 338 BC this king of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea. He had reformed the army with the long pike called the sarissa. He was assassinated in 336 by one of his bodyguards. For 10 points, name this father of Alexander.
This Epirote king won costly battles against Rome at Heraclea and Asculum in the 270s BC. His name gives us a phrase for a victory that costs too much. For 10 points, name this king.
In 202 BC the Romans under Scipio defeated Hannibal at this battle near Carthage. Masinissa's Numidian cavalry helped. It ended the Second Punic War. For 10 points, name this battle.

These two brothers, tribunes of the plebs in the 130s and 120s BC, proposed land reforms and were killed by senatorial mobs. Their opponents included Scipio Nasica, who led senators wielding stool legs against Tiberius. Their mother Cornelia was the daughter of Scipio Africanus. For 10 points, name these Roman reformers.

This Roman general reformed the army in 107 BC by recruiting landless citizens and held the consulship seven times. His rival Sulla marched on Rome. For 10 points, name this uncle of Julius Caesar by marriage.
This Roman dictator in 82 BC issued proscription lists to eliminate enemies. He retired in 79 BC. He was first to march on Rome with an army. For 10 points, name this man who defeated Marius.
Crassus died in 53 BC in this disastrous battle against Parthian cavalry and horse archers in Mesopotamia. The Romans lost their legionary standards. For 10 points, name this battle.

In 48 BC Julius Caesar defeated Pompey at this battle in Greece. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was killed. Caesar had about half as many men as his rival, and his troops broke the cavalry on the enemy flank. The battle took place on a plain near the Enipeus River. For 10 points, name this battle in Thessaly.
In AD 9 Arminius ambushed three Roman legions led by Publius Quinctilius Varus in this German woodland. Augustus is said to have cried, "Give me back my legions!" For 10 points, name this battle.
This queen of the Iceni led a revolt against Rome in AD 60 or 61. She burned Londinium and Camulodunum. She was defeated by Suetonius Paulinus. For 10 points, name this British queen.

This Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher wrote the Meditations while on campaign along the Danube. He was the last of the "Five Good Emperors." His son Commodus succeeded him. For 10 points, name this man.

In AD 212 an emperor of the Severan dynasty issued an edict extending Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire. He killed his brother Geta. For 10 points, name this emperor, for whom a famous set of baths in Rome is named.

In AD 378 Emperor Valens was killed at this battle in Thrace by Gothic cavalry. It showed the weakness of the Roman army. The emperor had refused to wait for reinforcements from his nephew Gratian. Two-thirds of the eastern field army perished in the fighting. For 10 points, name this battle named for a city.

In 451 the Romans and Visigoths under Aetius defeated this ruler of the Huns on the Catalaunian Plains. He later invaded Italy and was turned back from Rome. For 10 points, name this "Scourge of God."

In AD 476 this Germanic general deposed the last western Roman emperor Romulus Augustulus. He ruled Italy as king. He sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and nominally accepted the authority of Emperor Zeno. The deposed boy emperor was pensioned off in Campania. For 10 points, name this man.

This dynasty ruled much of the Yellow River valley from around 1600 BC. Its kings used oracle bones for divination and buried chariots in royal tombs at Anyang. For 10 points, name this dynasty that preceded the Zhou.

The Zhou kings justified overthrowing the Shang with this doctrine, saying that heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler. The idea was used by the Duke of Zhou to defend the conquest of King Wu. It was later applied to explain the rise and fall of later dynasties, which supposedly lost it through misrule. For 10 points, name this Chinese concept.

This Chinese general and strategist, said to have served the state of Wu, wrote a treatise on war containing the line "all warfare is based on deception." For 10 points, name this author of The Art of War.

This Han emperor ruled from 141 to 87 BC, expanded Chinese territory, sent Zhang Qian west, and established Confucianism as state doctrine. For 10 points, name this emperor whose name means "martial."

This Bronze Age city in the Indus Valley had a Great Bath, a grid plan, and drains. It was excavated in the 1920s in what is now Pakistan. For 10 points, name this city whose name means "mound of the dead."

This founder of the Mauryan Empire took power around 321 BC after the Nanda dynasty. He later became a Jain monk. His adviser Kautilya wrote the Arthashastra. For 10 points, name this emperor, grandfather of Ashoka.
This capital of the Assyrian Empire on the Tigris was destroyed in 612 BC by a Babylonian and Median alliance. It lies across the river from modern Mosul. For 10 points, name this city.

text: In 216 BC the consuls Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus led about 80,000 Romans against a smaller army in Apulia. Hannibal placed weaker Gallic and Spanish infantry in the center and let the Roman legions be surrounded by his cavalry and African infantry. Paullus died in the fighting. For 10 points, name this battle, a model of double envelopment.

In 331 BC Alexander the Great met the army of Darius III on a plain east of the Tigris. Scythed chariots failed against his phalanx, and Alexander led a cavalry charge at a gap in the enemy line. Darius fled and was later killed by Bessus. For 10 points, name this decisive battle that ended the Achaemenid Empire.

In 755 this general rebelled against the Tang court at the capital of Chang'an, nearly toppling the dynasty. He had been a favorite of Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guifei. For 10 points, name this rebel, whose name is An.

This Song dynasty chancellor, who served Emperor Shenzong, tried to reform government with measures like the Green Sprouts law. Conservatives under Sima Guang opposed him. For 10 points, name this statesman.
This Japanese novel, written around 1000 by a court lady, follows a prince in the Heian court. It is often called the world's first novel. For 10 points, name this work by Murasaki Shikibu.
In 1185 this man of the Minamoto clan defeated the Taira at Dan-no-ura and became the first shogun in 1192 of the Kamakura shogunate. His wife was Hojo Masako. For 10 points, name this man.

In 1260 the Mamluks under Baibars and Qutuz defeated a Mongol army at this battle in Palestine. It halted Mongol expansion into Egypt. For 10 points, name this battle whose name means "Spring of Goliath."
This Turco-Mongol conqueror, called "the Lame," built an empire from Samarkand around 1370 to 1405. He captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid at Ankara in 1402. For 10 points, name this man.

In 1526 Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at this battle north of Delhi, founding the Mughal Empire. He used gunpowder and cannon. The Mughal victory was helped by field artillery, which Ottoman advisers had taught Babur to use. The sultan of Delhi died on the field and the battle was fought on a plain. For 10 points, name this battle.

In 1514 the Ottomans under Selim I used cannon and muskets to defeat the Safavid Shah Ismail at this battle in eastern Anatolia. The Safavid cavalry lacked firearms and could not break the Ottoman janissaries behind wagons and cannon. Selim then briefly occupied Tabriz. For 10 points, name this battle.

This Safavid shah, who ruled from 1588 to 1629, moved the capital to Isfahan and defeated the Uzbeks and Ottomans. He is called "the Great." He used English adventurers like Robert Sherley to modernize his army with artillery. He also settled Armenian merchants in New Julfa near his new capital. For 10 points, name this ruler.

In 1757 Robert Clive defeated Siraj ud-Daulah at this battle in Bengal, helping establish East India Company rule. Clive had bribed the nawab's commander Mir Jafar to stay out of the fight. The nawab was later captured and killed, and Mir Jafar was installed. For 10 points, name this battle.
This Mughal emperor ruled from 1658 to 1707, expanded to the Deccan, and reimposed the jizya. His wars with the Marathas strained the empire. For 10 points, name this son of Shah Jahan.

This Maratha ruler carved out a Hindu kingdom in western India and was crowned chhatrapati in 1674. He fought Aurangzeb using guerrilla tactics. He escaped from Agra by hiding in a basket of sweets after being summoned by the Mughal emperor. He built a navy and many hill forts, such as Raigad. For 10 points, name this man.

This southern African stone city, built from the eleventh to fifteenth centuries by the Shona, has a Great Enclosure. Its name means "stone houses." For 10 points, name this site, which gave a modern country its name.
This queen of Ndongo and Matamba in Angola resisted Portuguese slave traders in the seventeenth century. She negotiated with Portugal and allied with the Dutch. For 10 points, name this woman.

In 1896 Ethiopian forces under Menelik II defeated an Italian army at this battle, preserving Ethiopian independence. The Italians had advanced in separate columns that lost contact, and about 70,000 Ethiopian soldiers overwhelmed them. Empress Taytu also took part in the campaign. For 10 points, name this battle in the Tigray highlands.
In 1898 Herbert Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army defeated the Mahdist forces of the Khalifa at this battle in Sudan. Winston Churchill took part as a cavalry officer. For 10 points, name this battle.
In 1898 Kang Youwei persuaded the Guangxu Emperor to launch a short-lived program of modernizing reforms, ended by Cixi. For 10 points, name this reform program, named for its length.

In 1919 students gathered in Tiananmen to protest the Treaty of Versailles' transfer of German rights in Shandong to Japan. It started a movement for a new culture. For 10 points, name this movement named for a month and a day.
In 1934 and 1935 about 100,000 Communist soldiers retreated from Jiangxi to northern Shaanxi, covering thousands of miles. Mao Zedong gained leadership. For 10 points, name this march.
In 1937 Japanese troops captured the Chinese capital and committed mass atrocities over six weeks. For 10 points, name this event, in a city on the Yangtze that was then Chiang Kai-shek's capital.

Mao launched this movement in 1966 to purge "revisionists." Young Red Guards attacked teachers and officials, and it lasted about a decade. Its leaders included the Gang of Four, and Liu Shaoqi died after being denounced. Schools were closed and intellectuals were sent to the countryside. For 10 points, name this upheaval.

In 1905 Admiral Togo destroyed the Russian fleet in this naval battle in a strait between Korea and Japan. It ended the Russo-Japanese War. The Russian Baltic Fleet had sailed all the way around Africa and Asia to get there. Nearly all its ships were sunk or captured in about two days. For 10 points, name this battle.
In 1955 leaders such as Nehru, Sukarno, Nasser, and Zhou Enlai met at this conference in Indonesia to promote nonalignment. For 10 points, name this conference named for a city in West Java.

This war, fought from 1954 to 1962, saw the FLN fight France for independence. Charles de Gaulle ended it with the Evian Accords. The conflict involved the torture of suspects, the Battle of Algiers, and a coup attempt by French generals. About a million colonists left the country afterward. For 10 points, name this war.

In 1952 this Kikuyu-led uprising against British colonial rule in Kenya began. Jomo Kenyatta was jailed. Rebels swore oaths and attacked white settlers and loyalist Africans. The British held tens of thousands in detention camps, and Dedan Kimathi was captured in 1956. For 10 points, name this rebellion.

In June 1967 Israel destroyed Egyptian air forces and captured Sinai, the Golan Heights, and the West Bank in this six-day conflict. It began with a surprise air strike on the morning of June 5. Jordan lost East Jerusalem, and the Suez Canal was closed until 1975. For 10 points, name this war.

This Cambodian Communist leader, born Saloth Sar, ruled from 1975 to 1979 and emptied cities. About two million died. He studied in Paris and led a regime that replaced money with forced labor on farms. Vietnam invaded to overthrow it in late 1978. For 10 points, name this leader of the Khmer Rouge.

In 1971 East Pakistan broke away from West Pakistan after a war in which India intervened. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman led the movement. The Awami League won the 1970 elections, but power was not transferred. Millions of refugees fled to India, and Dhaka became the capital of the new state. For 10 points, name this new country.
This Indonesian leader proclaimed independence from the Dutch in 1945 and was the first president. He promoted "Guided Democracy" before being displaced by Suharto. For 10 points, name this man.

In June 1989 the Chinese army crushed pro-democracy demonstrations in this Beijing square. The protests began after the death of Hu Yaobang, and the Goddess of Democracy statue was built there. A lone man stopped a column of tanks the next day. For 10 points, name this square, in front of the Forbidden City.

text: Thomas Sutpen's attempt to found a dynasty fails after his part-Black son Charles Bon is killed by his legitimate son Henry. Quentin Compson and his Harvard roommate Shreve piece the story together. For 10 points, name this novel set in Yoknapatawpha County by William Faulkner.

This novel is narrated in four sections, beginning with the thoughts of Benjy, who has an intellectual disability. Caddy Compson's loss of her virginity, Quentin's suicide at Harvard, and the servant Dilsey are central. For 10 points, name this William Faulkner novel.

A teenager called "the kid" joins the scalp-hunting Glanton gang, led in part by the philosophical and violent Judge Holden. Set in the American Southwest and Mexico in the 1850s, it has Biblical prose. For 10 points, name this novel by Cormac McCarthy, subtitled "The Evening Redness in the West."

Tyrone Slothrop, a US lieutenant, is tracked by a pattern of V-2 rockets falling on London. Characters in this postmodern novel include Pirate Prentice and Pointsman. For 10 points, name this novel by Thomas Pynchon.
Bigger Thomas works as a chauffeur for the Dalton family and accidentally smothers their daughter Mary. His lawyer Max defends him in court. For 10 points, name this novel by Richard Wright.

Macon "Milkman" Dead III tries to find gold with his friend Guitar and learns that his ancestors could fly. His aunt Pilate carries a box with her own name in her ear. For 10 points, name this novel by Toni Morrison.

The fisher king, the seer Tiresias, and the clairvoyant Madame Sosostris appear in this modernist poem, which opens "April is the cruellest month." It ends with a Sanskrit blessing, "Shantih shantih shantih." For 10 points, name this poem by T. S. Eliot in five parts.

This long poem begins "I saw the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness." It was first read at the Six Gallery in San Francisco and led to an obscenity trial of publisher Lawrence Ferlinghetti. For 10 points, name this poem by Allen Ginsberg.

Esther Greenwood interns at a New York magazine and later experiences a mental breakdown, undergoes electroshock treatment, and attempts suicide. For 10 points, name this semi-autobiographical novel by Sylvia Plath.

Newland Archer is engaged to May Welland, but falls in love with her cousin Ellen Olenska, who has returned to New York society after a failed marriage. For 10 points, name this novel by Edith Wharton.

Isabel Archer rejects Caspar Goodwood and Lord Warburton, then marries the manipulative Gilbert Osmond. Her cousin Ralph Touchett secretly arranges for her to inherit a fortune. For 10 points, name this novel by Henry James.

Jim Burden narrates the story of a Bohemian immigrant girl on the Nebraska prairie, whom he meets after moving in with his grandparents. She later works as a hired girl in Black Hawk and has many children after marrying Anton Cuzak. Her name is the title of this novel. For 10 points, name this novel by Willa Cather.

The Tyrone family spends a day in a summer house, as the mother Mary relapses into morphine addiction and the son Edmund learns he has tuberculosis. For 10 points, name this autobiographical play by Eugene O'Neill.

George and Martha, a history professor and his wife, have drunken fights while entertaining a younger couple, Nick and Honey, after a faculty party. They invent a son. For 10 points, name this play by Edward Albee.
A scrivener at a Wall Street law firm answers every request by saying, "I would prefer not to." He is eventually found dead in the Tombs. For 10 points, name this short story by Herman Melville.

Jurgis Rudkus and his wife Ona work in Chicago's Packingtown, where they endure miserable conditions in the meatpacking industry. Its depiction of unsanitary conditions led to food safety laws. For 10 points, name this muckraking novel by Upton Sinclair.

Kilgore Trout is a science-fiction author who appears in several of this author's works, and the narrator of this novel says that "So it goes" after every death. The hero marries Valencia and is displayed in a zoo on Tralfamadore with Montana Wildhack. He was a prisoner of war who survived the bombing of Dresden in a meat locker. For 10 points, name this novel by Kurt Vonnegut.

Captain Yossarian tries to avoid flying more missions, but a regulation says that anyone who wants to avoid combat is sane and so can be sent to fly. For 10 points, name this novel by Joseph Heller, whose title names that rule.

Sal Paradise travels across the United States with Dean Moriarty, a character based on Neal Cassady. This novel was typed on a continuous scroll of paper. For 10 points, name this Beat Generation novel by Jack Kerouac.

Chief Bromden narrates this novel set in a psychiatric ward in Oregon, where Randle McMurphy challenges the tyranny of Nurse Ratched. McMurphy organizes a fishing trip, and he is eventually given a lobotomy. Billy Bibbit stutters and kills himself after Ratched threatens to tell his mother. For 10 points, name this novel by Ken Kesey.
answer: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest

text: John Grimes, a young boy in Harlem, undergoes a religious conversion on his fourteenth birthday. His stepfather Gabriel is a preacher. For 10 points, name this semi-autobiographical novel by James Baldwin.
answer: Go Tell It on the Mountain

text: This poet wrote "Sunday Morning" and "The Emperor of Ice-Cream," and in one poem he advises that one must have "a mind of winter." He worked as an insurance executive in Hartford, Connecticut. For 10 points, name this author of "Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird."

This poet and physician from Paterson, New Jersey, led the Imagist movement with a poem that begins "so much depends upon a red wheel barrow." He also wrote the long poem Paterson. For 10 points, name this author of "This Is Just to Say."

In a story by this author, a grandmother is killed by the escaped convict the Misfit. She also wrote the novels Wise Blood and The Violent Bear It Away and was a Georgia Catholic. For 10 points, name this Southern Gothic author of "A Good Man Is Hard to Find."

Tommy Wilhelm is a failed salesman who loses his money on the commodities market in a novella by this author, set during a single day. He also wrote Herzog and Humboldt's Gift. For 10 points, name this Chicago author of The Adventures of Augie March.

Lily Bart falls from high society in New York and dies of an overdose of chloral. Her failure to marry Lawrence Selden or a wealthy man leaves her poor. For 10 points, name this novel by Edith Wharton.
A small-town girl travels to Chicago and becomes an actress, while the manager George Hurstwood, who stole money from his employer, declines. For 10 points, name this novel by Theodore Dreiser.

In this short story, the title character goes into the forest at night and sees the minister and his wife Faith at a witches' meeting. He is changed forever. For 10 points, name this story by Nathaniel Hawthorne.

This poet's Cantos were written over nearly five decades in the style of a modernist epic. He founded Imagism, edited Eliot's The Waste Land, and was held at a psychiatric hospital after supporting Mussolini. For 10 points, name this American expatriate poet.

Ignatius J. Reilly, an overweight and slothful man, goes on adventures in New Orleans after quitting his job. The author died by suicide and never saw it published; it won a Pulitzer Prize. For 10 points, name this novel by John Kennedy Toole.

The ambitious doctor Tertius Lydgate marries Rosamond Vincy, and Dorothea eventually marries Will Ladislaw. The author's real name was Mary Ann Evans. For 10 points, name this novel set in a provincial town, a work by George Eliot.

Becky Sharp climbs through society by marrying Rawdon Crawley, while her friend Amelia Sedley is loyal to the memory of George Osborne. William Dobbin loves Amelia faithfully. The Battle of Waterloo is part of this novel, subtitled "A Novel Without a Hero." For 10 points, name this work by William Makepeace Thackeray.

A black page mourns the death of the parson Yorick in this novel, whose narrator is not born until the third volume. Uncle Toby and his servant Corporal Trim reenact sieges on a bowling green. The title narrator's father, Walter, writes a treatise that he calls his "Tristrapaedia." For 10 points, name this digressive eighteenth-century novel by Laurence Sterne.
answer: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman

text: A foundling is raised by Squire Allworthy and is loved by Sophia Western. He is cast out after being falsely accused by the scheming Blifil. The author described this book as a "comic epic poem in prose." For 10 points, name this novel by Henry Fielding, whose hero is a foundling.
answer: The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling

text: A wedding guest is stopped by an old sailor, who says he killed an albatross. The ship is becalmed, and "Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink." Death and Life-in-Death play dice for the crew. For 10 points, name this poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge.
answer: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

text: This mock-epic poem is based on a real quarrel between the Petre and Fermor families. Belinda has a lock of hair cut off by the Baron while sylphs guard her, and the poem contains a card game of ombre. For 10 points, name this poem by Alexander Pope.

This novel takes place on June 16, 1904, and follows Stephen Dedalus and an advertising canvasser named Leopold Bloom around Dublin. It ends with the soliloquy of Bloom's wife Molly, and its chapters correspond to episodes in Homer's Odyssey. For 10 points, name this novel by James Joyce.

Lily Briscoe struggles to finish a painting while the Ramsay family vacations on the Isle of Skye. A middle section called "Time Passes" describes the house in decay during World War I. For 10 points, name this modernist novel by Virginia Woolf.

Estragon and Vladimir wait beside a bare tree for a man who never arrives, while Pozzo leads Lucky around on a rope. A boy arrives at the end of each of the two acts to say the man will not come today. For 10 points, name this play by Samuel Beckett.

The Redcrosse Knight travels with the lady Una and is deceived by the magician Archimago and by the false lady Duessa. This allegorical poem is written in a stanza with a final alexandrine and is dedicated to Elizabeth I. For 10 points, name this unfinished poem by Edmund Spenser.

After signing away his soul to the devil Mephistophilis, a scholar from Wittenberg summons Helen of Troy and asks "Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?" The Good Angel and Evil Angel urge him to repent. For 10 points, name this play by Christopher Marlowe.
alternates: The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus

text: In this play, a Venetian magnifico pretends to be dying so that the parasite Mosca can get gifts from the legacy hunters Voltore, Corbaccio, and Corvino. Celia is nearly raped. For 10 points, name this play by Ben Jonson, whose title character means "the fox."

This poet wrote that "No man is an island" and in one poem addressed a flea that has bitten both him and his lover. He was Dean of Saint Paul's Cathedral. He wrote "Death, be not proud" and "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning." For 10 points, name this metaphysical poet.

This Poet Laureate wrote an elegy for his friend Arthur Hallam titled "In Memoriam A. H. H." He also wrote "The Charge of the Light Brigade" and a cycle of poems based on the legends of Camelot. For 10 points, name this Victorian poet.

In this dramatic monologue, a Duke of Ferrara shows a visitor a portrait on his wall painted by Fra Pandolf. The Duke says that he "gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together." He then points out a statue of Neptune taming a seahorse. For 10 points, name this poem by Robert Browning.

This Jesuit priest developed "sprung rhythm" in poems such as "The Windhover" and "Pied Beauty." His poems were published posthumously by his friend Robert Bridges. For 10 points, name this author of "God's Grandeur."

This poet met Siegfried Sassoon at Craiglockhart War Hospital. He wrote "Strange Meeting" and a poem that calls "the old Lie" that it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country. He was killed one week before the Armistice. For 10 points, name this author of "Dulce et Decorum Est."

This poet wrote "Musee des Beaux Arts," which discusses the Icarus painting by Brueghel. He also wrote "Funeral Blues," which begins "Stop all the clocks," and "September 1, 1939." For 10 points, name this British-American poet.

This poet worked as a librarian at the University of Hull. He wrote "Church Going" and the collection The Whitsun Weddings. He admired Thomas Hardy and wrote "High Windows." For 10 points, name this author of "This Be the Verse."

Two minor characters from Hamlet wander through Elsinore flipping coins that keep coming up heads, and they are finally sent to their deaths in England. They are accompanied by a troupe of tragedians led by the Player. For 10 points, name this play by Tom Stoppard, whose title names the pair.

Charles Ryder narrates this novel as he returns to a country house where he once had a friendship with Sebastian Flyte. Lady Marchmain, Julia, and Cordelia belong to a Catholic family. The subtitle refers to "Sacred and Profane Memories." For 10 points, name this novel by Evelyn Waugh.

The whisky priest is hunted across Tabasco in Mexico by a lieutenant who wants to eradicate the Church. He fathered a daughter named Brigitta, and he is betrayed by the mestizo. For 10 points, name this novel by Graham Greene.

Doctor Aziz is accused of assaulting Adela Quested in the Marabar Caves. Fielding, the principal of a government college, is one of the few Englishmen to support him. For 10 points, name this novel by E. M. Forster.

Paul Morel is torn between his possessive mother Gertrude and his lovers Miriam Leivers and Clara Dawes. His father, Walter, is a coal miner in Nottinghamshire. For 10 points, name this semi-autobiographical novel by D. H. Lawrence.

Alex leads a gang of droogs who speak the slang Nadsat and commit "ultraviolence." He is later subjected to the Ludovico technique. The twenty-first chapter, in which Alex matures, was omitted from the American edition. For 10 points, name this novel by Anthony Burgess.

The interminable Chancery lawsuit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce hangs over this novel. Esther Summerson narrates half of it, and Lady Dedlock hides a secret about her past. Krook dies by spontaneous combustion, and Inspector Bucket investigates the murder of Tulkinghorn. For 10 points, name this novel by Charles Dickens.

A shipwrecked sailor from York spends twenty-eight years on an island off the coast of South America. He meets a native whom he names for the day of the week he was found. For 10 points, name this novel by Daniel Defoe about a castaway.

Jude Fawley, a stonemason, dreams of studying at Christminster but is thwarted by class barriers. He is entangled with Arabella Donn and with his cousin Sue Bridehead. Their son, nicknamed Little Father Time, kills their children and himself. For 10 points, name this novel by Thomas Hardy.

Basil Hallward paints a portrait of a handsome young man, who falls under the influence of Lord Henry Wotton. As he commits sins and ruins the actress Sibyl Vane, the picture ages in his place. For 10 points, name this novel by Oscar Wilde.

A butler named Stevens takes a motor trip across England in 1956, reflecting on his years of service to Lord Darlington and on his missed chance with the housekeeper Miss Kenton. For 10 points, name this novel by Kazuo Ishiguro.

text: Hans Castorp visits his cousin at a Swiss sanatorium in Davos and stays seven years. He debates the humanist Settembrini with the Jesuit Naphta and falls in love with Clavdia Chauchat. For 10 points, name this novel by Thomas Mann.
Gustav von Aschenbach, an aging writer, becomes obsessed with a Polish boy named Tadzio while he vacations in Venice during a cholera outbreak. For 10 points, name this novella by Thomas Mann.

Oskar Matzerath decides at age three to stop growing and plays a toy instrument. His voice can shatter glass, and he lives in Danzig during the rise of the Nazis. For 10 points, name this novel by Gunter Grass.

A bitter retired civil servant writes of the "underground" in the first part of this novella and in the second part describes how he humiliated a young prostitute named Liza. He rejects the "Crystal Palace" of rational utopias. For 10 points, name this novella by Fyodor Dostoevsky.
Evgeny Bazarov, a young nihilist, visits the Kirsanov family and fights a duel with Pavel Petrovich. He falls for Anna Odintsova and dies of typhus. For 10 points, name this novel by Ivan Turgenev.

The title character spends much of his time lying in bed, and his friend Stolz tries to rouse him. He loves Olga Ilyinskaya but marries his landlady, Agafya. For 10 points, name this novel by Ivan Goncharov.

Grigory Pechorin, an army officer, leads a trail of destruction, from kidnapping the Circassian girl Bela to killing Grushnitsky in a duel. The book is made up of five connected tales, including "Taman" and "The Fatalist." For 10 points, name this novel by Mikhail Lermontov.

Woland, the devil, arrives in Moscow with a retinue that includes the giant cat Behemoth. A parallel plot follows Pontius Pilate and the prisoner Yeshua Ha-Notsri, which is a novel written by the title writer. For 10 points, name this novel by Mikhail Bulgakov.

Shukhov's day begins when he wakes up in a prison camp in Siberia. He steals bread and earns an extra bowl of gruel. The novel was published in 1962 under Khrushchev. For 10 points, name this novel by Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn.
answer: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich

text: Professor Serebryakov and his young wife Elena visit an estate where Sonya and her uncle work to send them money. The doctor Astrov and Vanya both love Elena. Vanya fires a pistol at the professor and misses. For 10 points, name this play by Anton Chekhov.

On Midsummer Eve, the valet Jean seduces his master's daughter in the kitchen while the cook Kristin sleeps. The title character later is told by Jean to kill herself with his razor. For 10 points, name this naturalist play by August Strindberg.

Garcin, Ines, and Estelle are locked in a room furnished in Second Empire style and realize they are in hell. Garcin concludes that "Hell is other people." For 10 points, name this play by Jean-Paul Sartre.
Etienne Lantier becomes a miner at Montsou and joins a strike led by the Maheu family. The mine is flooded by the anarchist Souvarine. For 10 points, name this novel by Emile Zola.

Eugene de Rastignac lives in the Maison Vauquer boarding house, where the convict Vautrin tempts him and an old vermicelli maker is abandoned by his daughters Delphine and Anastasie. For 10 points, name this novel by Honore de Balzac.

Berenger watches as the inhabitants of a small town turn one by one into large animals. Jean transforms in front of him, and Daisy leaves with the herd. For 10 points, name this absurdist play by Eugene Ionesco.

Don Fabrizio, Prince of Salina, watches Garibaldi's landing in Sicily and arranges the marriage of his nephew Tancredi to Angelica, the daughter of a parvenu. It contains the famous idea that "everything must change so that everything can stay the same." For 10 points, name this novel by Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa.

This novel contains the openings of ten different books, which the Reader, in the second person, keeps trying to finish. He pursues Ludmilla, a woman he meets at a bookstore. For 10 points, name this postmodern novel by Italo Calvino.
answer: If on a Winter's Night a Traveler
alternates: If on a winter's night a traveller

text: Renzo and Lucia are prevented from marrying by the local lord Don Rodrigo. The novel, set in seventeenth-century Lombardy, includes a plague in Milan. For 10 points, name this novel by Alessandro Manzoni.

The assistant bookkeeper Bernardo Soares writes in a fragmentary prose, published after the author's death in 1935. The author wrote under many heteronyms, such as Alberto Caeiro and Alvaro de Campos. For 10 points, name this work by Fernando Pessoa set in Lisbon.

A man waiting in his car at a traffic light is suddenly struck by a sudden loss of sight, a "white" sickness, and the epidemic spreads through the city. Only the doctor's wife can still see. For 10 points, name this novel by Portuguese author Jose Saramago.

An unnamed writer starves in Kristiania while refusing help and chasing his pride. This novel was the breakthrough of Norwegian Nobel laureate Knut Hamsun. For 10 points, name this novel whose title means a physical need.

This sequence of ten poems was begun at a castle near Trieste and later finished in Switzerland. It begins "Who, if I cried out, would hear me among the angels' hierarchies?" For 10 points, name this work by Rainer Maria Rilke.
Paul Verlaine shot the author of this work in Brussels in 1873. It includes sections titled "Delirium" and "Alchemy of the Word." For 10 points, name this prose-poem sequence by Arthur Rimbaud.

The Bride runs away with Leonardo on her wedding day, and the Bridegroom and Leonardo kill each other in the forest. The Moon and Death appear as characters in this play. For 10 points, name this play by Federico Garcia Lorca.

William of Baskerville and his novice Adso investigate a series of murders at a Benedictine abbey in 1327. The blind monk Jorge hides a forbidden book of Aristotle, in a library that is a labyrinth. For 10 points, name this novel by Umberto Eco.

A canteen woman pulls her wagon across Europe during the Thirty Years' War, losing her children Eilif, Swiss Cheese, and the mute Kattrin. It is an example of epic theatre. For 10 points, name this play by Bertolt Brecht.

The Vicomte de Valmont and the Marquise de Merteuil compete to ruin Madame de Tourvel and the young Cecile Volanges. This epistolary novel was published in 1782. For 10 points, name this novel by Pierre Choderlos de Laclos.

A queen of Athens confesses her love for her stepson Hippolytus after her nurse Oenone persuades her. She hears a false rumor that her husband Theseus is dead. For 10 points, name this neoclassical tragedy by Jean Racine.

Two giants, a father and a son, are the title characters of this work. It describes the Abbey of Theleme, whose motto is "Do what thou wilt," and features the companion Panurge. For 10 points, name this work by Francois Rabelais.
In this anonymous Spanish picaresque novel from 1554, a boy leads a blind beggar, a stingy priest, and an impoverished squire. For 10 points, name this novel whose title character is a young servant.
alternates: La vida de Lazarillo de Tormes

text: This work opens with the sound of the bells of the Gion monastery echoing the impermanence of all things. It tells of the rise and fall of the Taira clan and of its defeat by the Minamoto at the sea battle of Dan-no-ura, where the child emperor Antoku drowns. It was recited by blind monks accompanied by the biwa. For 10 points, name this Japanese war tale.

This work by a lady-in-waiting to Empress Teishi consists of lists, such as "Hateful Things," and sharp observations of Heian court life. The author was a rival of Murasaki Shikibu. Its title refers to the object on which the author wrote. For 10 points, name this classic by Sei Shonagon.

Shimamura, a wealthy dilettante from Tokyo, visits a hot spring town to see the geisha Komako, and he is also drawn to the girl Yoko. The setting is in a mountain region with heavy winter snowfall. For 10 points, name this novel by Yasunari Kawabata.

A student befriends an older man he calls "Sensei," who later sends him a long confessional letter. The letter reveals that Sensei betrayed his friend K, who killed himself, and that Sensei decides to die after the death of the Meiji emperor. For 10 points, name this novel by Natsume Soseki, whose title means "heart."

The narrator, Oba Yozo, writes three notebooks about his life of hiding behind comic masks and descending into addiction. The book opens "Mine has been a life of much shame." Its author killed himself in 1948. For 10 points, name this novel by Osamu Dazai.

This author's works include Confessions of a Mask, The Temple of the Golden Pavilion, and the tetralogy The Sea of Fertility. In 1970, he and members of his private militia seized a military office in Tokyo, and he committed ritual suicide when the soldiers did not support his coup. For 10 points, name this Japanese author.

This novel is about 108 outlaws who gather in a marsh in Shandong under the leadership of Song Jiang. Lin Chong and Wu Song, who kills a tiger barehanded, are among the heroes. It is attributed to Shi Nai'an and is one of the four classic Chinese novels. For 10 points, name this novel, also translated as Outlaws of the Marsh.

Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei swear a brotherhood in a peach garden at the beginning of this novel. The strategist Zhuge Liang uses a ruse to borrow arrows, and Cao Cao is defeated at the battle of Red Cliffs. For 10 points, name this historical novel by Luo Guanzhong.

This author gave up medicine after seeing a slide of a Chinese man about to be executed. He wrote "A Madman's Diary" and "The True Story of Ah Q." His collection Call to Arms helped begin modern Chinese literature. For 10 points, name this author.

King Dushyanta falls in love with a hermit's foster daughter in a forest. A sage's curse makes him forget her, and he only recognizes his wife after a lost ring is found in a fish. Their son becomes the emperor Bharata. For 10 points, name this Sanskrit play by Kalidasa.

This author set many of his novels in the fictional South Indian town of Malgudi. His works include Swami and Friends, The Guide, and The Financial Expert. For 10 points, name this Indian author, whose brother R. K. Laxman drew the cartoons.

The twins Estha and Rahel return to their family house in Ayemenem in Kerala, years after their cousin Sophie Mol drowned. Their mother Ammu has a forbidden love affair with the untouchable carpenter Velutha. For 10 points, name this novel that won the 1997 Booker Prize, by Arundhati Roy.

Horacio Oliveira moves between Paris and Buenos Aires, searching for his lover La Maga. A "Table of Instructions" lets the reader read its chapters in two different orders. For 10 points, name this experimental novel by Julio Cortazar.

A dying Mexican businessman lies in bed in Mexico City, recalling his life as a soldier in the Revolution and as a corrupt political boss. The narrative uses three voices: first person, second person, and third person. For 10 points, name this novel by Carlos Fuentes.

This book's essays discuss the "Pachuco" and the figure of the Malinche, the Indigenous woman who aided Cortes. It argues that the Mexican psyche is masked by solitude and the idea of the "chingada." For 10 points, name this 1950 essay collection by Octavio Paz.

Urania Cabral returns to the Dominican Republic after thirty-five years to confront her father, a former senator under a dictator. The novel also follows the 1961 assassination of Rafael Trujillo. For 10 points, name this novel by Mario Vargas Llosa.

David Lurie, a professor of Romantic poetry in Cape Town, loses his job after an affair with his student Melanie Isaacs. He moves to the Eastern Cape, where his daughter Lucy is raped on her farm. For 10 points, name this novel by J. M. Coetzee.

A narrator returns to a village on the Nile after studying in England and learns about the mysterious Mustafa Sa'eed, who had affairs with several Englishwomen in London. For 10 points, name this postcolonial novel by the Sudanese author Tayeb Salih.
answer: Season of Migration to the North

text: A tapster who loses his palm-wine tapster journeys to Dead's Town to find him. The author wrote in a form of English based on his native Yoruba. For 10 points, name this novel by Amos Tutuola, which T. S. Eliot's publisher Faber released in 1952.

This collection of quatrains was written by a Persian astronomer and poet. Its English version by Edward FitzGerald contains lines such as "A Book of Verses underneath the Bough, / A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread--and Thou." For 10 points, name this work by Omar Khayyam.
Thirty birds led by the hoopoe cross seven valleys to find the king of the birds, the Simorgh. They discover that the name means "thirty birds." For 10 points, name this Persian Sufi poem by Attar.

On the battlefield at Kurukshetra, the warrior Arjuna despairs at fighting his kinsmen. His charioteer, who is Krishna in disguise, explains duty, devotion, and detachment from the fruits of action. For 10 points, name this Hindu scripture whose name means "Song of the Lord."

Seven Macaw is shot down by the twin brothers, who also trick the lords of Xibalba. After earlier tries with mud and wood, the gods create humans from maize. The manuscript was copied and translated by the Dominican friar Francisco Ximenez in Guatemala. For 10 points, name this sacred book.

The griot Balla Fasseke is the narrator of the story of a prince born to a "buffalo woman," Sogolon. The prince, who could not walk as a child, overcomes the sorcerer-king Sumanguru and founds the Mali Empire. For 10 points, name this epic of the Mandinka people about Sundiata Keita.
alternates: Sundiata: An Epic of Old Mali

text: The three plays of this trilogy are Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers, and The Eumenides. Orestes kills his mother Clytemnestra to avenge his father, and the Furies pursue him until Athena sets up a trial. For 10 points, name this trilogy by Aeschylus.

The god Dionysus lures King Pentheus to spy on the women of Thebes dressed as a woman, and Pentheus is torn apart. His mother Agave then proudly carries his head, thinking that it is a lion's. For 10 points, name this play by Euripides.

A man named Lucius, curious about magic, accidentally turns himself into a donkey. This Latin novel contains the tale of Cupid and Psyche. For 10 points, name this novel, also titled the Metamorphoses, by Apuleius.

This collection of sayings and conversations, compiled by disciples, includes the line "Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself." It describes the ideal "gentleman" or junzi. For 10 points, name this collection of the teachings of Confucius.

The twins Pedro and Pablo Vicario kill Santiago Nasar because Angela Vicario named him as the man who took her virginity. The narrator investigates the case twenty-seven years later. For 10 points, name this novella by Gabriel Garcia Marquez.

Antoinette Cosway grows up in Jamaica after the end of slavery and marries an unnamed Englishman, who renames her Bertha. This novel is a prequel to Jane Eyre. For 10 points, name this novel by Jean Rhys.

This Tang dynasty poet lived through the An Lushan Rebellion and wrote of the line "The nation is broken, yet mountains and rivers remain." He was a friend of Li Bai and is often called the "poet-historian." For 10 points, name this Chinese poet.

text: The hacker Henry Case is hired by Armitage and teams up with Molly Millions to work with the AI called Wintermute. The novel begins with the sky "the color of television, tuned to a dead channel." For 10 points, name this cyberpunk novel by William Gibson.

Genly Ai is an envoy sent to the planet Gethen, whose inhabitants are ambisexual and become male or female during a period called kemmer. He travels across a glacier with the exiled Estraven. For 10 points, name this novel by Ursula K. Le Guin.

The psychologist Kris Kelvin arrives at a space station orbiting an ocean planet and finds that the ocean generates replicas of people from his memory, including his dead lover Harey. For 10 points, name this novel by Stanislaw Lem.

Valentine Michael Smith is raised by Martians and brought to Earth, where he introduces the word "grok." He founds a church whose members share water. For 10 points, name this novel by Robert Heinlein.

The Albertian Order of Saint Leibowitz preserves relics of twentieth-century knowledge in a desert monastery after a nuclear war. Brother Francis finds a fallout shelter containing a blueprint. For 10 points, name this novel by Walter M. Miller Jr.

Rick Deckard is a bounty hunter who retires rogue androids, using the Voigt-Kampff test to identify them. He also visits Rachael Rosen, and his wife Iran uses a mood organ. For 10 points, name this novel by Philip K. Dick that was adapted into Blade Runner.

alternates: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep

text: Hiro Protagonist is a pizza deliverer and a samurai swordsman who explores a virtual world called the Metaverse. He teams up with a skateboard courier named Y.T. to stop a virus. For 10 points, name this novel by Neal Stephenson.

This 1962 book opens with "A Fable for Tomorrow," about a town where birds no longer sing. It documents the effects of pesticides like DDT on the environment. For 10 points, name this book by Rachel Carson.

The author discusses "the problem of the color-line" and the concept of "double consciousness" in a collection of essays published in 1903. It includes a critique of Booker T. Washington. For 10 points, name this work by W. E. B. Du Bois.

This 1776 pamphlet argues that it is absurd for an island to rule a continent. It called for American independence in plain language and sold over a hundred thousand copies. For 10 points, name this pamphlet by Thomas Paine.

The narrator invents Judith Shakespeare, the equally gifted sister of William, to illustrate how women have been denied the freedom to write. The essay states that "a woman must have money and a room of her own." For 10 points, name this essay by Virginia Woolf.

This 1963 text was written in the margins of a newspaper and addressed to eight white clergymen. It declares that "injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere." For 10 points, name this letter by Martin Luther King Jr.

The frontispiece shows a giant crowned figure composed of many small people. It argues that without a sovereign, life in a state of nature would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." For 10 points, name this 1651 work of political philosophy by Thomas Hobbes.

Raphael Hythloday describes an island society without private property, which is the setting of this 1516 book. Its title comes from Greek words for "no place." For 10 points, name this work by Thomas More.

Written for Lorenzo de' Medici, this work argues that it is better for a ruler to be feared than loved, if one cannot be both. It discusses virtu and fortuna and cites Cesare Borgia as a model. For 10 points, name this political treatise by Niccolo Machiavelli.

This 1729 satire suggests that impoverished Irish families could sell their children as food for the rich. Its straight-faced narrator calculates the cost of fattening them. For 10 points, name this essay by Jonathan Swift.

This prose pamphlet was written in 1644 in opposition to a licensing law. It argues that "who kills a man kills a reasonable creature" but that destroying a good book kills reason itself. For 10 points, name this defense of free speech by John Milton.

Milo, a bored boy, drives a toy car through a tollbooth and visits Dictionopolis and Digitopolis. He travels with the watchdog Tock and the Humbug to rescue Rhyme and Reason. For 10 points, name this children's book by Norton Juster.

Mole, Rat, Badger, and a wealthy but reckless motorcar enthusiast live along a river in England. The stoats and weasels take over Toad Hall during Toad's imprisonment. For 10 points, name this children's novel by Kenneth Grahame.

Wendy, John, and Michael Darling fly with a boy from their nursery window to Neverland. There they meet Tinker Bell and the pirate Captain Hook, who fears a crocodile that swallowed a clock. For 10 points, name this play and novel by J. M. Barrie.

A robin leads a girl to a buried key, and with the gardener Ben Weatherstaff she restores a locked and neglected place on the Yorkshire moors. The child is orphaned by a cholera outbreak in India and finds her bedridden cousin Colin crying in the night. For 10 points, name this novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett.

Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert, siblings in Avonlea, adopt a red-haired orphan by mistake. She insists that her name be spelled with an "e" and later rivals Gilbert Blythe in school. For 10 points, name this novel by L. M. Montgomery, set on Prince Edward Island.

Dorothy is swept away from Kansas by a cyclone and lands in a magical country. In the book, as opposed to the film, she wears silver shoes and meets the Tin Woodman, the Scarecrow, and the Cowardly Lion. For 10 points, name this novel by L. Frank Baum.

Philip Marlowe is hired by General Sternwood to deal with a blackmailer involved with his daughter Carmen. Her sister Vivian is married to Rusty Regan, who has disappeared. For 10 points, name this 1939 novel by Raymond Chandler.

A diamond stolen from a statue in India is given to Rachel Verinder on her eighteenth birthday, and disappears. Sergeant Cuff investigates, and Franklin Blake turns out to have taken it under the influence of opium. For 10 points, name this novel by Wilkie Collins.

This poetic form has six stanzas of six lines each followed by a three-line envoi. The end words of the first stanza are repeated in a set pattern in the other stanzas. Elizabeth Bishop wrote a famous one about a grandmother and a child. For 10 points, name this form.

This interlocking rhyme scheme, in which the second line of a three-line stanza rhymes with the first and third of the next, was used by Dante in the Divine Comedy. Percy Shelley used it in "Ode to the West Wind." For 10 points, name this rhyme scheme.

This form, used in Persian and Urdu poetry, is made of couplets that each end with a repeated refrain. The poet often includes his or her own name in the final couplet. Hafez and Ghalib wrote these. For 10 points, name this form.

This metrical line has five feet, each consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one. When unrhymed, it is called blank verse and was used by Shakespeare and Milton. For 10 points, name this meter.

This narrative form of poetry was originally sung, and is usually composed of quatrains that rhyme ABCB. Examples include "Sir Patrick Spens" and "Barbara Allen." For 10 points, name this form, which gives its name to a collection by Wordsworth and Coleridge.

text: This Titan was tricked into swallowing a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes in place of his youngest son. He had earlier castrated his own father with a sickle given to him by his mother. He was later overthrown by his son and imprisoned in Tartarus or sent to the Isles of the Blessed, depending on the source. For 10 points, name this Titan, the father of Zeus and the Roman Saturn's counterpart.

In Hesiod's Theogony, this goddess arose after Chaos and bore Uranus without a mate. She helped her son Cronus castrate Uranus and later sheltered Zeus from his father. She was also the mother of Typhon. For 10 points, name this primordial Greek personification of the earth.

This monster had a hundred serpent heads that flashed fire from their eyes and produced the voices of many animals. He and Echidna were the parents of Cerberus, the Chimera, and the Hydra. Zeus defeated him with thunderbolts and buried him beneath Mount Etna. For 10 points, name this monster, the last challenger to Zeus's rule.

Hesiod says this goddess received honors from Zeus above all others, and she was a daughter of the Titan Perses and Asteria. She carries torches and is associated with crossroads, dogs, and witchcraft. She heard the cries of Persephone and helped Demeter search for her. For 10 points, name this triple-formed goddess of magic.

This hunter was changed into a stag after he accidentally saw a goddess bathing in a stream. His own hounds failed to recognize him and tore him apart. His teacher, the centaur Chiron, later mourned him with a statue. For 10 points, name this grandson of Cadmus.

This giant hunter was blinded by King Oenopion after a drunken assault on the king's daughter. He regained his sight after traveling east and facing the rising sun. A scorpion sent by Gaia or Hera killed him, and he was placed among the stars. For 10 points, name this hunter, a lover of Eos in some accounts.

This youth was born to Myrrha after she was transformed into a tree. Aphrodite and Persephone fought over him, and Zeus decided he would spend part of the year with each. He died after being gored by a boar, and the anemone grew from his blood. For 10 points, name this beautiful mortal.

This son of Theseus and an Amazon spurned the advances of his stepmother, who then accused him falsely. After Theseus cursed him, a bull sent by Poseidon frightened his horses and he was dragged to death. For 10 points, name this devotee of Artemis, the title character of a play by Euripides.

This daughter of King Minos gave Theseus a ball of thread to escape the Labyrinth. He abandoned her on Naxos, where she was found by Dionysus. The god set her wedding crown among the stars. For 10 points, name this wife of Dionysus.

This son of Tantalus was restored to life by the gods after he was cooked and served to them. His shoulder, eaten by Demeter, was replaced with ivory. He won his bride by cheating Oenomaus in a chariot race. For 10 points, name this man who gave his name to the southern part of mainland Greece.

This man killed his mother and her lover, Aegisthus, to avenge his father. The Furies pursued him until a trial on the Areopagus, where Athena cast the deciding vote for his acquittal. His sister Electra urged him on. For 10 points, name this son of Agamemnon.

This queen of Mycenae killed her husband in his bath after his return from Troy, citing the sacrifice of their daughter. She ruled with her lover Aegisthus, and was killed by her own son. She was the sister of Helen. For 10 points, name this wife of Agamemnon.

Calchas told Agamemnon to sacrifice this girl so that the winds would blow and the fleet could sail. Artemis replaced her with a deer at the altar and spirited her away to Tauris. For 10 points, name this daughter of Agamemnon, sacrificed at Aulis.

This Greek archer was bitten by a snake on the way to Troy, and his festering wound was so foul-smelling that the Greeks abandoned him on Lemnos. He possessed the bow of Heracles, which was needed to take Troy. For 10 points, name this title character of a Sophocles play.

This priest of Apollo warned the Trojans not to bring the wooden horse into the city and hurled a spear at it. Two sea serpents then crushed him and his sons. For 10 points, name this priest, whose agony is shown in a famous Hellenistic sculpture.

This nymph kept Odysseus on the island of Ogygia for seven years, offering him immortality if he stayed. Hermes ordered her to release him, and she supplied him with materials to build a raft. For 10 points, name this daughter of Atlas.

This blind prophet of Thebes was changed into a woman for seven years after striking two snakes. He told Odysseus how to get home when the hero consulted him in the Underworld. Hera blinded him for siding with Zeus in an argument. For 10 points, name this seer.

This queen of Pherae volunteered to die in place of her husband Admetus. Heracles wrestled Thanatos for her and brought her back from death. For 10 points, name this title character of a play by Euripides.

At this man's birth, the Fates said he would live only until a log in the fire burned up, so his mother Althaea snatched it out. Later, in anger over the killing of her brothers, she threw it back into the flames. He led the Calydonian boar hunt. For 10 points, name this Aetolian hero.

This king of the Lapiths murdered his father-in-law and was purified by Zeus, then tried to seduce Hera. Zeus tricked him with a cloud shaped like Hera, which gave birth to the centaurs. For 10 points, name this man, punished by being bound to a burning wheel.

This son of Helios begged his father to let him drive the sun chariot for a day. He lost control of the horses, scorching the earth, until Zeus killed him with a thunderbolt. He fell into the river Eridanus, and his sisters became poplar trees. For 10 points, name this hubristic youth.

This satyr picked up an aulos that Athena had thrown away, then challenged a god to a music contest. After losing, he was flayed alive and his blood became a river. For 10 points, name this satyr, a victim of Apollo.

This queen of Thebes boasted of her many children, claiming they surpassed those of Leto. Apollo and Artemis killed her children with arrows, and she turned into a rock that wept constantly. For 10 points, name this mother.

This Cypriot sculptor carved an ivory statue of a perfect woman and fell in love with it. After he prayed to Aphrodite, the statue came to life. For 10 points, name this king and artist, whose myth is told in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

Zeus and Hermes, disguised as travelers, were turned away from a thousand homes before being welcomed by this elderly Phrygian couple. The gods flooded the countryside but spared them, and they were turned into intertwining trees. For 10 points, name this couple, famous for hospitality.

This king of the Rutuli was a suitor of Lavinia, whom he sought to marry despite her betrothal to a Trojan. He was spurred on by the fury Allecto and by Amata. In the last scene of the Aeneid, he is killed by Aeneas. For 10 points, name this opponent of Aeneas.

This Arcadian king ruled the settlement of Pallanteum on the Palatine hill and gave Aeneas allies against the Latins. His son Pallas was killed by Turnus. For 10 points, name this king who welcomed Aeneas to the future site of Rome.

This queen of Troy was given as a slave to Odysseus after the war. In Euripides's play, she blinded the Thracian king Polymestor in revenge for the murder of her youngest son. For 10 points, name this wife of Priam.

This goddess of strife threw a golden apple inscribed to the fairest at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, because she had not been invited. The apple led to the Judgment of Paris. For 10 points, name this goddess whose Roman counterpart is Discordia.

This Titaness gave birth to the nine Muses after sleeping with Zeus for nine nights in a row. She was the personification of memory, and poets invoked her help in recalling the past. For 10 points, name this mother of the Muses.

text: After her father Thjazi was killed by the gods, this giantess armed herself and went to Asgard to seek compensation. The gods let her choose a husband by looking only at their feet, and she picked Njord thinking he was Baldr. She is said to have placed a venomous snake over the head of the bound Loki. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess of winter and the hunt.

This goddess's golden hair was cut off by Loki as a prank, and he had to get dwarves to forge a replacement of real gold. She is the wife of Thor and the mother of Thrud. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess.
This god's tongue is carved with runes, and he is a skald and the husband of Idun. He welcomes arrivals in Valhalla and is a god of poetry and eloquence. For 10 points, name this Norse god.

This silent son of Odin and the giantess Grid is the god of vengeance. At Ragnarok, he avenges his father by placing a thick shoe on the lower jaw of Fenrir and tearing it apart. He survives the destruction to rule in the new world. For 10 points, name this god.

This son of Odin and Rind was born for one purpose: to avenge the death of Baldr. He grew to full size in a single day and killed the god who threw the mistletoe, without washing his hands or combing his hair until he did so. For 10 points, name this god.
This stepson of Thor is the god of archery, skiing, and winter. He is a skilled hunter and used a bone as a ski, according to Saxo. His name means glory. For 10 points, name this god, a son of Sif.

This sea giant hosts the gods at a feast in the poem Lokasenna, where Loki insults all the guests. He and his wife Ran gather drowned sailors in a net. The gods needed a large cauldron to brew ale for his feast. For 10 points, name this Norse personification of the sea.

This giant owned a cauldron a mile deep, which Thor and Tyr obtained for Aegir. On a fishing trip with Thor, he cut the line when the hero hooked the world serpent, which used an ox head as bait. For 10 points, name this giant, the father of Tyr in some accounts.

This giantess was seen by Freyr from Odin's seat, and he fell so deeply in love that he stopped eating. His servant Skirnir won her over with threats and gifts, including the golden apples. She finally agreed to meet him after nine nights. For 10 points, name this giantess.

This dwarf lived in a waterfall in the form of a pike until he was caught by Loki. He gave up his gold hoard and ring, but he laid a curse on them. The curse affected Fafnir and Sigurd. For 10 points, name this dwarf, owner of the ring Andvaranaut.

After her husband Sigurd's murder, this woman was married to Atli, the king of the Huns. She killed the two sons she bore him and served them to their father, then killed Atli. For 10 points, name this Burgundian princess, whose brothers Gunnar and Hogni were involved in her first husband's death.

This father of Sigurd drew a sword from the tree Barnstokkr, where Odin had thrust it at a wedding feast. He eventually fought Odin in battle, who shattered the sword with his spear. For 10 points, name this Volsung hero.

The pieces of this sword, broken in Odin's battle, were reforged by Regin for Sigurd. Sigurd tested it by splitting an anvil, and used it to kill Fafnir. For 10 points, name this blade, a Norse equivalent of Nothung.

This being was created when the Aesir and Vanir sealed a truce by spitting into a jar. He was so wise that he could answer any question, but the dwarves Fjalar and Galar killed him and mixed his blood with honey. For 10 points, name this man, whose blood became the mead of poetry.

Odin spent three nights with this giantess to gain three drinks of the mead of poetry. Her father Suttung had hidden the mead inside a mountain and set her to guard it. For 10 points, name this giantess.

A giant disguised as a builder offered to rebuild Asgard's wall in a single winter, aided by this stallion, who hauled the stones with amazing strength. The gods forced Loki to stop him, and Loki then gave birth to a famous horse. For 10 points, name this stallion.
These three women live by a well at the roots of Yggdrasil and decide the fates of all beings. Their names are Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld. For 10 points, name these Norse equivalents of the Fates.

This loyal woman held a bowl over the head of her bound husband to catch the venom dripping from a serpent. When the bowl filled, the venom would drip on his face and cause earthquakes. For 10 points, name this wife of Loki.

This giant had a stone head and heart, and a stone shield. He challenged Thor to a duel after boasting in Asgard, and a clay giant named Mokkurkalfi was built to help him. A fragment of his whetstone remained lodged in Thor's head. For 10 points, name this giant.

Thor went to this giant's home without his hammer, belt, or gloves, borrowing the belt and iron gloves and a staff from the giantess Grid. The giant threw a molten iron bar at Thor, who caught it. For 10 points, name this giant, who was killed by Thor.

In this poem of the Poetic Edda, a seeress recounts the creation of the world to Odin and foretells its end. She describes the death of Baldr and the events of Ragnarok. For 10 points, name this poem whose title means prophecy of the seeress.

This Icelandic author of the thirteenth century wrote the Prose Edda, which preserves much of what we know of Norse myth. He also compiled Heimskringla, a history of Norwegian kings. For 10 points, name this historian and politician.

Odin describes hanging for nine nights on a windswept tree, stabbed with a spear, in this poem of the Poetic Edda. It consists mostly of proverbs and advice to travelers. For 10 points, name this poem whose title means sayings of the High One.

In the beginning, this great void lay between the fire world of Muspelheim and the ice world of Niflheim. Where the heat met the frost, life formed. For 10 points, name this yawning void, the primordial emptiness of Norse cosmology.

This Vanir sorceress was pierced with spears and burned three times in Odin's hall, yet she lived. Her treatment is said to have started the war between the Aesir and the Vanir. For 10 points, name this seeress.

This son of Odin rode Sleipnir for nine days and nights through dark valleys to the realm of the dead. There he pleaded with the ruler for the release of Baldr, and he brought back gifts such as the ring Draupnir. For 10 points, name this messenger god.
Freya obtained this necklace by spending a night with each of four dwarves. Loki stole it, and Heimdall fought him in the form of a seal to retrieve it. For 10 points, name this necklace.

This wife of Baldr died of grief when she saw his body, and her heart broke at his funeral. She was placed on his pyre aboard the ship Hringhorni, and she later joined him in the world after Ragnarok. For 10 points, name this goddess.

In a contest of wits with Odin, who traveled in disguise, this wise giant asked riddles about the world's beginning. He lost when Odin asked what he had whispered in his son's ear. For 10 points, name this giant.
