text: This Persian polymath born near Bukhara wrote the Canon of Medicine, which was used in European universities for centuries. His Book of Healing covers logic, physics, and metaphysics. His "floating man" thought experiment argues for the soul. For 10 points, name this philosopher, known in the West as Avicenna.

This Andalusian judge from Cordoba wrote the Incoherence of the Incoherence in reply to al-Ghazali. His commentaries on Aristotle made him known in Latin Europe as "the Commentator." For 10 points, name this philosopher, also called Ibn Rushd.

This Persian scholar left a teaching post in Baghdad after a spiritual crisis and wrote a work that attacked the philosophers on twenty points. His Revival of the Religious Sciences links law and mysticism. For 10 points, name this author of The Incoherence of the Philosophers.

This fourteenth-century scholar from Tunis wrote the Muqaddimah, an introduction to history. He discussed asabiyyah, or group solidarity, as a force that rises and declines in dynasties. For 10 points, name this historian.

This Moroccan traveler of the fourteenth century journeyed for nearly thirty years across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. He dictated an account called the Rihla and visited Mali and China. For 10 points, name this man.

This thirteenth-century poet was born in Balkh and settled in Konya after meeting the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz. His six-volume Masnavi is a major work of Persian literature. For 10 points, name this poet whose followers founded the Mevlevi order.

This Kurdish sultan of Egypt and Syria defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin in 1187 and recaptured Jerusalem. He founded the Ayyubid dynasty and later made a treaty with Richard the Lionheart. For 10 points, name this ruler.

This first major battle between the Muslims and Quraysh took place in 624 near a well in the Hejaz. About three hundred Muslims defeated a force more than three times as large. For 10 points, name this battle named for the site.

After this 625 battle near a mountain north of Medina, the Muslims suffered losses when archers left their posts and Muhammad was wounded. Hamza was killed. For 10 points, name this battle that followed Badr.

This 636 battle on a river in Syria saw Khalid ibn al-Walid's Muslim army defeat the Byzantines of Heraclius. It opened the way to the conquest of Syria. For 10 points, name this battle named for a tributary of the Jordan.

In 628 Muhammad signed this treaty with the Quraysh, allowing Muslims to make pilgrimage the following year and promising a ten-year truce. Some of his followers considered it humiliating, but the Quran calls it a clear victory. For 10 points, name this treaty.

This dynasty claimed descent from Fatima and ruled in Tunisia and Egypt, founding Cairo in 969 and the al-Azhar mosque. It belonged to the Ismaili branch of Shia Islam. For 10 points, name this caliphate.

This empire, founded by Osman, captured Constantinople in 1453 under Mehmed II. At its height under Suleiman it spread across the Balkans, Anatolia, and Arab lands. For 10 points, name this empire whose sultans were also caliphs.

This dynasty, founded by Ismail I in 1501, made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran. It built a capital at Isfahan under Shah Abbas. For 10 points, name this dynasty, rivals of the Ottomans.

This eighteenth-century reformer from the Najd preached strict monotheism and attacked tomb veneration. He allied with Muhammad ibn Saud in 1744. For 10 points, name this figure whose followers are called Wahhabis.
This Hanbali jurist, born in Harran in 1263, wrote fatwas against the Mongols and the excesses of Sufism. His ideas influenced later reformers. For 10 points, name this scholar of Damascus.

This Sunni school of law, the oldest and most widely followed, was founded by a scholar of Kufa who stressed analogy and reason. It dominated the Ottoman Empire and is followed in Turkey and South Asia. For 10 points, name this school, named for Abu Hanifa.
This largest Shia branch holds that the line of imams ended with the twelfth, who is in hiding. Iran and Iraq are home to most of its followers. For 10 points, name this branch, also called Imamiyya.
This Shia branch split from the Twelvers over the succession of Ismail, son of Jafar al-Sadiq. The Aga Khan leads one group, the Nizari. For 10 points, name this branch, also called the Seveners.

Shia Muslims believe that this figure, the twelfth imam, entered a state of occultation in the ninth century. He is expected to return and bring justice. For 10 points, give this title, also used in Sunni belief for a messianic deliverer.

This theological school, popular under the early Abbasids, held that the Quran was created and that human reason can know good and evil. It was favored by al-Mamun during the Mihna. For 10 points, name this rationalist school.

This Arabic word, meaning "oneness," names the central doctrine of Islam: that God is one and has no partners. Surah 112, al-Ikhlas, is regarded as a summary of it. Violating it is the sin of shirk. For 10 points, give this term.

This independent legal effort, from a root meaning "to strive," involves a scholar using reasoning to reach a ruling. Traditional scholars say its "gate" was closed, but modernists reject that. For 10 points, name this concept.

This former Ethiopian slave, a companion of Muhammad, became the first muezzin. According to tradition he was tortured in Mecca, with a heavy rock laid on his chest in the heat, for refusing to renounce his faith. He was freed by Abu Bakr and was known for his beautiful voice. For 10 points, name this man.

This building is known for its horseshoe arches and a forest of columns in a city in Andalusia. It was begun by Abd al-Rahman I and later turned into a cathedral. For 10 points, name this Andalusian mosque-cathedral.

This Sufi mystic of Baghdad, executed in 922, proclaimed "I am the Truth." He was accused of heresy and crucified. He studied under Junayd, wrote the Kitab al-Tawasin, and traveled widely before his trial. For 10 points, name this man.
This Andalusian mystic, called "the greatest master," wrote the Meccan Revelations. His doctrine of the unity of being influenced later Sufis. For 10 points, name this author of Bezels of Wisdom.
This wife of Muhammad, daughter of Abu Bakr, was said to have been nine at her marriage. She narrated many hadith and led forces at the Battle of the Camel in 656. For 10 points, name this woman.
This religious opinion, issued by a mufti, is a nonbinding ruling on a question of Islamic law. A famous example was issued against Salman Rushdie in 1989. For 10 points, give this term.

text: This agreement of 622 or 623, drawn up by Muhammad soon after the Hijra, regulated relations among Muslims, Jews, and pagan tribes of a certain city. It declared the signatories one community, or ummah, and set rules for blood money and mutual defense. It is regarded as an early written constitution. For 10 points, name this document, named for its city.

This second-century Indian philosopher wrote the Mulamadhyamakakarika, which argues that all phenomena lack inherent existence. He founded the Madhyamaka school and is often called the "second Buddha" in Tibet. For 10 points, name this Mahayana thinker whose name contains the word for serpent beings.

This Buddhist concept, often translated as "emptiness," holds that things have no independent essence. The Heart Sutra states that form is this and this is form. For 10 points, give this Sanskrit term central to Madhyamaka.

This collection of early Buddhist scriptures, whose name means "Three Baskets," is divided into the Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma. The Theravada school preserves it in Pali. For 10 points, name this canon.

This Mahayana scripture, translated into Chinese by Kumarajiva, teaches that all beings can attain Buddhahood. It contains parables such as the burning house. Nichiren Buddhists chant its title. For 10 points, name this sutra.

This thirteenth-century Japanese monk taught that the Lotus Sutra alone offered salvation. He chanted "Namu Myoho Renge Kyo" and predicted a Mongol invasion. For 10 points, name this founder of a Buddhist school named for him.

This Japanese Pure Land teacher, a disciple of Honen, taught that faith in Amida Buddha alone brings rebirth in the Pure Land. He married and founded the Jodo Shinshu tradition. For 10 points, name this monk.
This eighth-century Indian tantric master is said to have subdued demons and founded the first monastery at Samye in Tibet. Tibetans call him Guru Rinpoche. For 10 points, name this man.

This fourteenth-century Tibetan reformer founded the Gelug school and Ganden Monastery. He wrote the Lamrim Chenmo, a graded path to enlightenment. For 10 points, name this teacher whose school produced the Dalai Lamas.

This Tibetan text, often called the Tibetan Book of the Dead, describes the intermediate state between death and rebirth. It is read aloud to the dying. For 10 points, give this title, from a word for the "liberation through hearing."
This semi-legendary Indian monk is said to have arrived in China around 500 and sat facing a wall for nine years at Shaolin. He is credited with founding Chan Buddhism. For 10 points, name this man.

This seventh-century Chinese monk traveled to India, studied at Nalanda, and returned with hundreds of Sanskrit texts. His journey was the basis of the novel Journey to the West. For 10 points, name this pilgrim.
This Indian emperor's Rock Edicts promote dhamma after the carnage of the Kalinga war. He sponsored the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra. For 10 points, name this Mauryan ruler.
This Hindu philosophical school, developed by Shankara, teaches non-dualism: Brahman alone is real and the world is illusion. For 10 points, name this school of Vedanta, from Sanskrit for "not two."

This eleventh-century South Indian philosopher taught that Brahman is a personal God with the world and souls as his body. He founded the Vishishtadvaita school. For 10 points, name this Vaishnava theologian.

This Indian sage compiled aphorisms on the eight limbs of yoga, including yama, niyama, asana, and samadhi. The text is organized in four chapters, or padas, and defines yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind. For 10 points, name this author of the Yoga Sutras.

This Hindu festival, held every twelve years in rotation at four sites including Prayagraj and Haridwar, draws millions who bathe at river confluences. For 10 points, name this gathering named for a pot.
This Hindu festival lasts nine nights and honors the goddess in forms such as Durga. It ends with Dussehra, which celebrates the victory of Rama over Ravana. For 10 points, name this festival.

This black-skinned Hindu goddess is shown with a garland of skulls, a protruding tongue, and standing on Shiva. She is associated with time and destruction and worshipped in Kolkata. For 10 points, name this form of the Mother Goddess.

This Bengali mystic, a priest at Dakshineswar, taught that all religions lead to God. He worshipped the goddess Kali and, according to his biographers, spent time practicing Islam and Christian devotion. His disciple Vivekananda spread his message in the West. For 10 points, name this holy man.

This Hindu monk addressed the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago, beginning "Sisters and brothers of America." He founded the Ramakrishna Mission. For 10 points, name this disciple of Ramakrishna.

This Chinese philosopher's namesake book includes the story of the butterfly dream and the cook who carves oxen. He argued for spontaneity and relativity of viewpoints. For 10 points, name this Daoist, second to Laozi.

This Confucian philosopher argued that human nature is good and compared its tendencies to sprouts. He lived in the fourth century BCE and told of a mother who moved three times to educate him. For 10 points, name this "second sage."

This Confucian argued that human nature is bad and must be shaped by ritual and education. His students included the Legalists Han Fei and Li Si. For 10 points, name this third-century BCE philosopher.

This Song dynasty scholar synthesized Confucian ideas with metaphysics, emphasizing li and qi and the Four Books. His commentaries became the basis of civil service exams. For 10 points, name this Neo-Confucian.

This ancient Chinese divination text consists of sixty-four hexagrams made of broken and unbroken lines. Confucian tradition adds commentaries called the Ten Wings. For 10 points, name this "Book of Changes."

This Japanese collection of 712, compiled by Ō no Yasumaro, tells the creation of the islands by Izanagi and Izanami. It is the oldest surviving Shinto-related chronicle. For 10 points, name this book.

This sun goddess of Shinto hid in a cave, plunging the world into darkness, until she was lured out by a dance and a mirror. The imperial family claims descent from her. For 10 points, name this kami.

This Jain sect's monks go without clothes, while the other main sect wears white robes. In their tradition, Mahavira never married and women cannot attain liberation directly. Its name means "sky-clad." For 10 points, name this group, contrasted with the Svetambara.

This fifth Sikh guru compiled the Adi Granth and built the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar. According to tradition he invited the Muslim saint Mian Mir to lay the temple's foundation. He was executed by the Mughal emperor Jahangir. For 10 points, name this first Sikh martyr.

text: This collection of 423 verses in the Pali Canon, attributed to the Buddha, begins "Mind is the forerunner of all things." It is organized in twenty-six chapters including those on the mind, the thousands, and the monk. It is among the most widely read and translated Buddhist texts. For 10 points, name this anthology.

This pharaoh, born Amenhotep IV, moved the capital to Amarna and promoted the worship of the sun disk. He closed temples of Amun and left behind the Great Hymn to the sun. Nefertiti was his queen. For 10 points, name this Eighteenth Dynasty ruler, father of Tutankhamun.

This sun disk, depicted with rays ending in hands, was the sole god promoted by a pharaoh who built a capital at Akhetaten. For 10 points, name this deity, whose worship replaced the cult of Amun for a time.

This medieval dualist movement in southern France, centered on Albi and Toulouse, taught that the material world was evil. Its adherents, the "perfecti," were persecuted in a crusade launched by Innocent III in 1209. For 10 points, name this heresy, also called Albigensian.

This twelfth-century merchant of Lyon gave away his wealth to preach in poverty and had his teachings condemned in 1184. His followers, who rejected purgatory, later joined the Protestant churches. For 10 points, name this namesake of a movement.

This Czech priest of Prague, influenced by Wycliffe, preached in the Bethlehem Chapel and was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415. His followers started the Hussite Wars. For 10 points, name this reformer.

This small religious community, still living at Mount Gerizim near Nablus, accepts only its own version of the Torah. It considers itself the true Israel and offers Passover sacrifices. For 10 points, name this group.

This Gnostic-influenced group of southern Iraq and Iran reveres John the Baptist and uses baptism in flowing water. Their scripture is the Ginza Rabba, written in a dialect of Aramaic. For 10 points, name this group.

This seventeenth-century Jewish mystic from Smyrna declared himself the Messiah in 1665 and converted to Islam under pressure from the Ottoman sultan. For 10 points, name this man whose followers were called Sabbateans.

This Chinese man, who failed the civil service exam, claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus. He led a rebellion from 1850 and founded the Heavenly Kingdom in Nanjing. For 10 points, name this leader of the Taiping.

This Swedish scientist wrote Heaven and Hell after a series of visions in 1745. Followers who founded the New Church believed in correspondences between spiritual and natural worlds. For 10 points, name this man.

This celibate communal sect, formally the United Society of Believers, was led in America by Ann Lee. It is known for ecstatic dancing, simple furniture, and a hymn "Simple Gifts." For 10 points, name this group.
This Vermont preacher founded a community in New York in 1848 based on "complex marriage" and communal living. It later made silverware. For 10 points, name this man who founded the Oneida Community.
This Russian-born cofounder of the Theosophical Society wrote Isis Unveiled and The Secret Doctrine. She claimed contact with hidden Masters in Tibet. For 10 points, name this woman.

These sisters of Hydesville, New York, claimed in 1848 to communicate with a spirit through knocking sounds. Their claims started the Spiritualist movement. For 10 points, give this surname of the sisters.

This Native American Church uses a cactus containing mescaline as a sacrament. Its buttons are chewed or brewed into tea, and the church was incorporated in Oklahoma in 1918. Its meetings are held in a tipi and last all night. For 10 points, name the plant used.

This Plains ceremony, held in the summer and involving fasting and dancing around a central pole, is sometimes accompanied by piercing. The Lakota call it wiwang wacipi. For 10 points, name this ritual.

This text of the K'iche' Maya recounts the creation and the adventures of the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, in the underworld Xibalba. It was transcribed in the Latin alphabet in the sixteenth century and copied by the Dominican friar Francisco Ximenez. For 10 points, name this book.

This Inca sun god was worshipped at the Coricancha in Cusco. His temple was said to be lined with sheets of gold, and a festival at the June solstice honored him. The Inca emperor claimed descent from him. For 10 points, name this deity.
This indigenous religion of Tibet, older than Buddhism, has priests who perform funerals and rituals. Its followers now often use Buddhist-like monasteries. For 10 points, name this religion.
This sky god worshipped by Turks and Mongols was called Eternal Blue Sky. The Khans claimed his mandate. For 10 points, name this deity whose religion was practiced by Genghis Khan's people.

This divination system of the Yoruba uses a palm nut tray and sixteen principal figures called odu. The deity Orunmila presides over it, and Ile-Ife in Nigeria is regarded as its center. Its priests are called babalawo. For 10 points, name this system.
This Afro-Brazilian religion, with houses called terreiros, honors orixas such as Oxala and Iemanja. It developed in Bahia among Yoruba-descended enslaved people. For 10 points, name this religion.

This religion of Lebanon, Syria, and Israel developed from Ismaili Shia Islam in the eleventh century. It venerates the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim and does not accept converts. For 10 points, name this group.
This Vietnamese religion founded in 1926 blends Buddhism, Confucianism, Christianity, and spiritism. Its Holy See is in Tay Ninh, and its symbol is an eye. For 10 points, name this religion.
This Japanese new religion, founded by Nakayama Miki in 1838, centers on a pillar called Jiba in a town near Nara. Followers believe in God the Parent. For 10 points, name this religion.

This English civil servant published Witchcraft Today in 1954 and helped found modern Wicca. He wrote High Magic's Aid and claimed initiation by a woman named Dorothy Clutterbuck. He claimed to be initiated into a New Forest coven. For 10 points, name this man.
This 1961 merger of two American denominations created a liberal religion with no creed. It lists seven principles, including the inherent worth of every person. For 10 points, name this faith.

This Bengali teacher, born Abhay Charan De, founded the International Society for Krishna Consciousness in New York in 1966. He translated the Bhagavad Gita with commentary. For 10 points, name this swami.
This American organization, led by Elijah Muhammad, taught that Wallace Fard Muhammad was Allah in person. Malcolm X was one of its ministers before leaving in 1964. For 10 points, name this group.

This New York farmer predicted that Christ would return in 1843 or 1844. His calculation drew on the 2300 days in the Book of Daniel. His followers, called by his surname, experienced the Great Disappointment. For 10 points, name this man.

This Jamaican activist founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association and promoted "Back to Africa." Rastafari revere him as a prophet. He founded the Black Star Line and was deported from the United States in 1927 after a mail fraud conviction. For 10 points, name this man.

text: This enzyme complex's alpha and beta subunits spin a central gamma stalk as protons flow through its membrane-embedded Fo portion. Paul Boyer proposed a binding change mechanism for it, and John Walker determined its structure. It is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and thylakoid membrane. For 10 points, name this enzyme that makes the main energy currency of the cell from ADP and phosphate.

These cellular structures are made of ribosomal RNA and proteins in large and small subunits, and the 80S version is found in eukaryotes. The peptidyl transferase activity is carried out by the rRNA, making them ribozymes. They have A, P, and E sites for tRNA. For 10 points, name these organelles where translation occurs.

Barbara McClintock discovered these mobile genetic elements in maize, noting that they caused variegated kernel colors by moving between positions in the genome. Class I types move through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase, while class II types use a cut-and-paste mechanism with transposase. She received a Nobel Prize in 1983 for this work. For 10 points, name these "jumping genes."

This process in eukaryotes occurs in the nucleus, where RNA polymerase II synthesizes pre-mRNA. Introns are removed by the spliceosome after it. A TATA box in the promoter is recognized by general initiation factors before it starts. For 10 points, name this process by which a DNA sequence is copied into messenger RNA.

Meselson and Stahl showed that DNA replication has this property by growing bacteria on nitrogen-15 and then nitrogen-14 and examining bands in a cesium chloride gradient. After one generation all DNA was of intermediate density. Each new double helix contains one old strand and one new strand. For 10 points, name this model of replication, as opposed to conservative or dispersive.

This organelle has a double membrane with folds called cristae and contains its own circular DNA. It is the site of the Krebs cycle and most ATP production in eukaryotic cells. Lynn Margulis popularized the endosymbiotic theory for its origin. For 10 points, name this "powerhouse of the cell."

This hormone from the anterior pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol. It is cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin along with beta-endorphin. Its release is stimulated by corticotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus. For 10 points, name this hormone abbreviated ACTH.

The Hardy-Weinberg principle states that allele frequencies stay constant in the absence of mutation, gene flow, genetic drift, natural selection, and non-random this activity. The principle's equation is p squared plus two p q plus q squared equals one. For 10 points, name this activity, which in Hardy-Weinberg must be random, referring to choosing partners.

This process of cell division produces four genetically distinct haploid cells and includes crossing over in prophase I. It is used to make gametes in animals. Its two successive divisions are called I and II, and the first one reduces the chromosome number. For 10 points, name this type of division, distinct from mitosis, though its name looks similar.

This molecule has a cloverleaf secondary structure and carries an amino acid on its 3-prime end, with an anticodon loop that pairs with mRNA. Aminoacyl synthetases charge it. It was first described by Robert Holley, who sequenced one for alanine. For 10 points, name this adapter in translation, abbreviated tRNA.

This signaling molecule's cyclic form, abbreviated cAMP, was discovered by Earl Sutherland as a second messenger. It is produced from ATP by adenylyl cyclase after a G protein-coupled receptor is activated. For 10 points, name this second messenger that activates protein kinase A.

This 1952 experiment used bacteriophages labeled with radioactive sulfur and phosphorus to show that DNA, not protein, is the genetic material. It was carried out by two researchers at Cold Spring Harbor. For 10 points, name this experiment named for its two scientists, with a blender.

This type of bond holds the two strands of DNA together, joining adenine to thymine with two of them and guanine to cytosine with three. They are weak individually but strong in number. For 10 points, name this bond, which also holds water molecules together.

These cells in the immune system produce antibodies after maturing from B cells. They have an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum, enabling high protein secretion. For 10 points, name these cells whose name refers to the fluid part of blood plus the term for cell.

This disease is caused by a single glutamic acid to valine substitution in the beta chain of hemoglobin. Heterozygous carriers have resistance to malaria, an example of heterozygote advantage. Deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerizes, deforming red blood cells. For 10 points, name this genetic disease with a crescent-shaped cell.

This enzyme, discovered in thermophilic bacteria from Yellowstone, is used in PCR because it survives denaturation temperatures. Kary Mullis developed the technique that uses it. For 10 points, name this heat-stable DNA polymerase, whose name comes from Thermus aquaticus.

This organ of the human body filters blood to produce urine, using functional units called nephrons. Humans typically have two of them, located near the lower back. For 10 points, name this organ whose failure requires dialysis.

This man proposed a system of binomial nomenclature in his Systema Naturae, giving each species a genus and species name. He is called the father of taxonomy. For 10 points, name this Swedish botanist, whose name is often Latinized as Linnaeus.

This phase of the cell cycle contains the restriction point, where cells commit to division, and is regulated by the retinoblastoma protein and cyclin D. Cells that exit the cycle enter a resting state, G zero, from it. For 10 points, name this first gap phase, preceding S phase.

These biomolecules are polymers of amino acids and fold into primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structures. Alpha helices and beta sheets are examples of secondary structure in them. Enzymes are mostly these. For 10 points, name this class of macromolecule.

This is the process by which water vapor leaves the stomata of plants. It creates a pull that draws water up the xylem from the roots. For 10 points, name this plant process whose name combines "trans" and a word for breathing out.

This Danish physician developed a stain that distinguishes bacteria by cell wall structure, resulting in purple and pink cells. Gram-positive bacteria retain crystal violet because of thick peptidoglycan. For 10 points, name this man whose name is attached to the stain.

This type of natural selection favors both extreme phenotypes over the intermediate one, which can lead to a bimodal distribution. It differs from stabilizing and directional selection. For 10 points, name this type of selection, whose name suggests a rupture.

This molecule is the final electron acceptor in the aerobic electron transport chain, forming water at cytochrome c oxidase. Its absence slows oxidative phosphorylation. For 10 points, name this gas, which humans breathe in.
This group of plants, which includes pines and firs, bear seeds in cones and have needle-like leaves. They are gymnosperms. For 10 points, name this group named for their cone-bearing habit.

This protein, a tumor suppressor sometimes called the "guardian of the genome," halts the cell cycle after DNA damage, and is mutated in about half of all cancers. Li-Fraumeni syndrome arises from a germline mutation of its gene. For 10 points, name this protein named for its molecular weight in kilodaltons.

This process in bacteria transfers DNA through a pilus from a donor with an F plasmid to a recipient. It is one of three ways that bacteria exchange genetic material along with transformation and transduction. For 10 points, name this process, a bacterial analogue of mating.

This is the basic unit of heredity, a segment of DNA that codes for a protein or functional RNA. Mendel called it a factor, and Wilhelm Johannsen coined the modern word. Alleles are alternative versions of it. For 10 points, name this unit located at a specific locus on a chromosome.

This neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction and binds nicotinic receptors on muscle cells. Its breakdown is by acetylcholinesterase, and it is blocked by curare. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter with an abbreviation ACh.

This cycle in the mitochondrial matrix begins when acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate, catalyzed by citrate synthase. It produces NADH, FADH2, and GTP while releasing two carbon dioxide molecules per turn. Hans Krebs described it in 1937. For 10 points, name this cycle, also called the citric acid cycle.

text: This process converts atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia over an iron catalyst at high temperature and pressure, roughly 200 atmospheres. Carl Bosch scaled it up industrially at BASF. It made synthetic fertilizers possible and also supplied explosives for World War I. For 10 points, name this process developed by a German chemist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize.

This rule predicts that when hydrogen bromide adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen attaches to the carbon that already bears more hydrogens. It is explained by the greater stability of the more substituted carbocation. A Russian chemist from Kazan proposed it in 1869. For 10 points, name this regioselectivity rule.

These elements, with atomic numbers 57 through 71, fill the 4f subshell and are usually shown in a detached row beneath the main periodic table. They have very similar chemical properties, which made them hard to separate, and cerium is the most abundant of them. Many are used in strong magnets and phosphors. For 10 points, name this series of rare-earth elements that begins with lanthanum.

In this type of reaction, an electron pair is donated by a nucleophile to a carbon bearing a leaving group. The first, called SN1, goes through a carbocation, while the second, SN2, is concerted with inversion of configuration. For 10 points, name this reaction type, abbreviated with an S and a N.

This is the most abundant element in the universe and the lightest element, with an atomic number of one. Its most common isotope has no neutron. It makes up most of the mass of the Sun. For 10 points, name this element with symbol H.

These elements, found in group 18, have filled valence shells and are therefore largely unreactive. Neil Bartlett made the first compound of one with platinum hexafluoride. For 10 points, name this group, including helium, neon, and argon.

This quantum number, symbolized l, determines the shape of an orbital, with s, p, d, and f corresponding to values 0 through 3. It is also called the azimuthal quantum number. For 10 points, name this quantum number, named for the angular momentum of the electron.

This equation, PV equals nRT, relates pressure, volume, amount, and temperature for a hypothetical type of gas that has no intermolecular forces. For 10 points, name this equation of state, for a "perfect" kind of gas.
This type of bond involves the sharing of electron pairs between two atoms, as in the molecule of water. It typically forms between nonmetals. For 10 points, name this bond, distinct from ionic.

This law states that the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same regardless of the pathway, as long as initial and final conditions are the same. It is named for a Swiss-born Russian chemist. For 10 points, name this law for adding enthalpies.

This reaction between a conjugated diene and a dienophile forms a six-membered ring in a concerted pericyclic process. Otto Diels and Kurt Alder shared the 1950 Nobel Prize for it. For 10 points, name this cycloaddition reaction.

In this process, an electrolyte solution undergoes a nonspontaneous reaction when current is passed through it. Michael Faraday formulated laws for it, and it is used to produce aluminum and chlorine. For 10 points, name this process, a use of electrical energy to drive chemistry.

This acid, with formula HCl, is found in the human stomach and is also used for cleaning metal. It is a strong acid that dissociates completely in water. For 10 points, name this acid, with a name referring to a chlorine-containing hydrogen compound.

This scientist's model of the atom, proposed in 1913, has electrons in quantized circular orbits and explains the spectrum of hydrogen. He later headed an institute in Copenhagen and won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. His principle of complementarity was debated with Einstein. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist.

This equation relates the rate constant of a reaction to temperature as k equals A times e to the negative E a over R T. It shows that rates increase exponentially with temperature. For 10 points, name this equation from a Swedish chemist.

These are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and so different mass numbers. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are examples, and the latter is used in radiocarbon dating. Hydrogen has three common ones, including deuterium and tritium. For 10 points, name this term.
This is the term for the minimum energy required for a reaction to proceed, represented by the height of the barrier on an energy diagram. Catalysts lower it. For 10 points, name this energy.

This rule says that electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing up. For example, in a p subshell, three electrons occupy three different orbitals. For 10 points, name this rule named for a German physicist.

This type of isomerism occurs when two molecules are non-superimposable mirror images, as in L and D amino acids. A carbon with four different groups is called a center of this. For 10 points, name this property of "handedness."

This scale, from zero to fourteen, uses the concentration of hydronium ions to measure acidity; solutions below seven are acids. For 10 points, name the quantity that equals the negative log of hydrogen ion concentration.

This family of organic compounds contains a carbonyl group bonded to a hydrogen and an R group, as in formaldehyde and acetaldehyde. They are oxidized to carboxylic acids. For 10 points, name this functional group.

This law relates the absorbance of light by a solution to its concentration, the path length, and a molar absorptivity. Spectrophotometers rely on it to find concentrations from a calibration curve. It is named for a German physicist and for a Swiss-German mathematician, joined by a hyphen. For 10 points, name this absorbance law.

This is the process of a solid changing directly into a gas without passing through the liquid phase. Dry ice does this at room temperature and ordinary pressure, as does iodine when heated gently. Its reverse is called deposition. For 10 points, name this phase change.

This element has atomic number 79 and symbol Au, from the Latin aurum. It is dense, malleable, and unreactive, dissolving only in aqua regia, a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids. Rutherford's famous scattering experiment used foil made of it. For 10 points, name this precious metal.

This law states that the pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of each component. It is named for an English chemist who also proposed an atomic theory. For 10 points, name this law named for a man who also studied color blindness.
This is the term for a substance, often a metal such as platinum, that speeds up a reaction without being consumed. Enzymes act as biological examples. For 10 points, name this term.

This element, with atomic number 8, is necessary for combustion and respiration. It makes up about a fifth of Earth's atmosphere, and its allotrope ozone forms a protective layer high above. Joseph Priestley and Carl Scheele both isolated it. For 10 points, name this element with symbol O.

This family of organic compounds has a hydroxyl group bonded to a saturated carbon. The simplest, with one carbon, is methanol. For 10 points, name this functional group, such as ethanol in beverages.
This principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers. It was formulated by an Austrian physicist. For 10 points, name this principle.

This type of compound consists of a central metal atom or ion bound to surrounding ligands, as in cisplatin and the heme group. Alfred Werner won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining their structure. For 10 points, name this class of compounds with a central metal atom and attached ligands.

text: This effect, explained by Einstein in 1905, occurs when light of sufficiently high frequency ejects electrons from a metal surface. The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on frequency but not intensity. Below a threshold frequency, no electrons are emitted regardless of brightness. For 10 points, name this effect that supports the particle nature of light.

This quantity for a rotating body equals the product of its moment of inertia and its angular velocity. It is conserved when no net external torque acts, which is why a spinning figure skater speeds up when pulling in her arms. Kepler's second law reflects its conservation. For 10 points, name this rotational analogue of linear momentum.

This law states that the induced electromotive force in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through it. It underlies electric generators and transformers. For 10 points, name this law of electromagnetic induction named for an English scientist.

This experiment, performed in 1887 by Albert Michelson and Edward Morley, attempted to detect the motion of Earth through a hypothetical medium for light. It found no difference in the speed of light with direction. For 10 points, name the medium that this experiment failed to detect, a "luminiferous" substance.

This is the SI unit of electrical resistance, equal to one volt per ampere. It is symbolized by the Greek letter omega. For 10 points, name this unit named for a German physicist who formulated a law relating voltage, current, and resistance.

This principle says that the buoyant force on an object immersed in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. It explains why steel ships can float and was supposedly discovered in a bathtub. For 10 points, name this principle named for a Greek scientist of Syracuse.

This phenomenon occurs when waves bend as they pass around obstacles or through openings comparable in size to their wavelength. It produces the patterns seen in single slit experiments and in X-ray crystallography. For 10 points, name this phenomenon that distinguishes waves from particles in classical physics.

This type of wave has particles vibrating perpendicular to the direction of travel, like waves on a rope. Light is an example. For 10 points, name this wave type contrasted with longitudinal waves such as sound.

This equation, discovered by a Scottish physicist in the 1860s, is actually a set of four equations unifying electricity, magnetism, and light. It predicted electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light. For 10 points, name these equations named for James Clerk Maxwell.

This principle states that along a streamline in steady flow of an ideal fluid, an increase in speed comes with a decrease in pressure. It is used to explain the operation of a Venturi tube and the lift on a wing. It was published in Hydrodynamica by a member of a Swiss family of mathematicians. For 10 points, name this principle.

This is the term for the bending of light as it passes from one medium into another, described by Snell's law. It explains why a straw looks bent in a glass of water and why a pool seems shallower than it is. It occurs because light changes speed. For 10 points, name this phenomenon.

This physicist's equation, a partial differential equation, describes how the quantum state of a system changes with time, with the Hamiltonian operator. He shared the 1933 Nobel Prize with Paul Dirac. For 10 points, name this Austrian physicist who also proposed a cat thought experiment.

This number, equal to the ratio of speed of light in vacuum to the speed in a medium, is always at least one. Water has a value of about 1.33. For 10 points, name this number that determines how much light bends.

This is the force that a stretched or compressed object exerts to return to its shape, described by Hooke's law. It is proportional to displacement. For 10 points, name this force exerted by a coil on a toy slinky, or one that bounces a car.

This particle, discovered by Carl Anderson in 1932, has the same mass as an electron but opposite charge. Dirac's equation predicted its existence. When it meets an electron, both are annihilated into gamma rays. For 10 points, name this antimatter counterpart of the electron.

This phenomenon causes the observed frequency of a wave to differ from the emitted frequency when the source and observer are in relative motion. It explains the change in pitch of a passing siren. For 10 points, name this effect named for an Austrian physicist.

This type of energy is associated with motion and equals one half mass times velocity squared. A moving car has a large amount of it, and the work-energy theorem says the net work done on an object equals its change in this quantity. Raising an object converts it into potential energy. For 10 points, name this energy of motion.

This thermodynamic law states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. It implies that heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold. For 10 points, name this law, often numbered as the second.

This 1911 discovery by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes found that mercury's resistance drops abruptly to zero below about four kelvin. Such materials expel magnetic fields in the Meissner effect. For 10 points, name this phenomenon of zero electrical resistance at low temperatures.

This type of lens is thicker in the middle than at its edges and bends parallel rays of light toward a focal point. Magnifying glasses and the lenses of eyeglasses for farsighted people use it. The human eye has one made of a flexible tissue. For 10 points, name this converging lens, whose name suggests an outward curve.

This is the term for a particle that carries the strong force between quarks, binding them into protons and neutrons. It is a massless boson that carries color charge, and its exchange is described by quantum chromodynamics. Its name suggests a sticky substance. For 10 points, name this gauge boson.

This is the lowest-energy state of a quantum harmonic oscillator, whose energy is nonzero, equal to half of Planck's constant times frequency. It is a consequence of the uncertainty principle. For 10 points, give this term, also used for the energy of the vacuum.

These are the three laws proposed by Johannes Kepler for the motion of planets, including that orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus. For 10 points, what is the general name of these laws, relating a planet's orbital period to its distance from the Sun?
This is the bending of light caused by passing through a prism, which splits white light into a spectrum. Newton studied this. For 10 points, name this separation of light by wavelength.

This is the term for the maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium position. For sound, it determines loudness, and for light, it determines brightness. The energy carried by a wave is proportional to its square. For 10 points, name this property of a wave, the height of a crest.

This physicist found that nuclear fission in uranium could produce a self-sustaining chain reaction, and directed the first nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, in 1942. He won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this Italian-American physicist.

In this quantum effect a particle passes through a potential barrier that it classically lacks the energy to cross. George Gamow used it to explain alpha decay, and it makes scanning probe microscopes and flash memory work. The probability falls off exponentially with barrier width. For 10 points, name this effect.

This is the term for the bending of a path of light by a massive object, predicted by general relativity and observed in the eclipse of 1919. For 10 points, name this effect, which creates Einstein rings.

text: In this effect, discovered by an American physicist in 1923, X-rays scattered from electrons emerge with longer wavelength than the incident beam. The wavelength shift depends on the scattering angle. It could not be explained by classical wave theory and showed that photons carry momentum. For 10 points, name this effect named for Arthur Holly.

This blue glow seen in the water surrounding nuclear reactor cores occurs when charged particles travel faster than light does in that medium. It is analogous to a sonic boom. It is named for a Soviet physicist who shared the 1958 Nobel Prize. For 10 points, name this radiation.

This boundary in the Earth separates the mantle from the outer core at a depth of about 2,900 kilometers. S waves cannot pass through the layer below it, which showed that the outer core is liquid. Beno Gutenberg discovered it in 1914. For 10 points, name this discontinuity named for the German-American seismologist.

This Milankovitch-related cycle describes changes in the shape of Earth's orbit around the Sun, varying between nearly circular and mildly elliptical over about 100,000 years. Along with axial tilt and precession, it is thought to pace ice ages. For 10 points, name this orbital parameter whose value measures how elongated an orbit is.

This Austrian-born geologist proposed that continents were once joined in the supercontinent Pangaea and drifted apart. His hypothesis lacked a mechanism and was rejected until plate tectonics. For 10 points, name this German meteorologist.

This fine-grained dark rock makes up most of the oceanic crust and builds the Hawaiian volcanoes. It is low in silica and rich in iron and magnesium. Columnar jointing in it forms the Giants Causeway in Northern Ireland. For 10 points, name this common volcanic rock.

This scale ranks minerals from one to ten based on their ability to scratch one another, with talc at one and diamond at ten. It was created by a German geologist in 1812. For 10 points, name this scale.

These large waves are generated by earthquakes under the seafloor and travel across the ocean at speeds near 800 kilometers per hour. They grow in height as they reach shallow water. For 10 points, name this kind of wave whose name is Japanese for "harbor wave."

This layer of the Earth lies between the crust and core and makes up most of the planet's volume. It convects slowly and drives plate motion. For 10 points, name this largely solid layer rich in the mineral olivine.

This is the process in which rock is broken down into smaller pieces and carried away by wind, water, and ice. Rivers carve canyons like the Grand Canyon through it. For 10 points, name this process distinct from weathering that moves sediment.

This is the point on Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake. Seismologists locate it by triangulating the arrival times of P and S waves from at least three stations. For 10 points, name this point.

This type of plate boundary occurs where two plates move toward each other, with one plate sliding under another. It creates deep ocean trenches like the Mariana Trench and volcanic arcs. For 10 points, name this process and boundary type.
This is the name for molten rock that has erupted onto the surface of the Earth. Hawaiian volcanoes produce a lot of it. For 10 points, name this material that cools to form basalt.

Sandstone, limestone, and shale are examples of this rock class, which forms when sediments are compacted and cemented together over time. Fossils are most commonly found in it, and it often shows distinct layers called strata. Unlike igneous and metamorphic rocks, it forms at or near the surface. For 10 points, name this rock class.

This scale measures the magnitude of earthquakes using the logarithm of amplitude recorded on a seismograph. A tenfold increase in amplitude corresponds to one unit. For 10 points, name this scale named for a California seismologist, now replaced by the moment magnitude scale.

This type of rock forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting. Marble comes from limestone and slate from shale in this process. For 10 points, name this rock class, whose name means "change of form."
This gas, making up about 78 percent of Earth's atmosphere, is the most abundant gas in it. Plants cannot use it directly, and bacteria fix it. For 10 points, name this element with symbol N.

This is the layer of the atmosphere containing the ozone layer, lying above the troposphere. Temperature rises with altitude in it because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. For 10 points, name this layer.

This process is the transfer of water vapor to the atmosphere from plants. Together with evaporation it is called evapotranspiration. For 10 points, name the process by which plants release water vapor through leaf pores.

These deposits of unsorted sediment, from clay to boulders, are left behind by glaciers. Terminal ones mark the farthest advance of the ice, and Long Island and Cape Cod were formed from them. Lateral and medial types form along the sides and between merging glaciers. For 10 points, name these glacial deposits.

This is the term for the dense, hot, mostly iron and nickel center of the Earth. It has a solid inner part and a liquid outer part, and the motion of the liquid generates the planet's magnetic field. Its radius is a little over 3,000 kilometers. For 10 points, name this innermost layer.

This is the long ocean ridge system where new crust is created by seafloor spreading. The Mid-Atlantic one runs down the Atlantic. Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading. For 10 points, name this feature at a divergent boundary.
This relative dating principle states that in undisturbed sedimentary rock sequences, the oldest layers are at the bottom. It was proposed by Nicolas Steno. For 10 points, name this principle.

This is the name for the shaking of the ground caused by a sudden release of energy along a fault. The San Andreas fault produces many in California, and the 1906 one in San Francisco destroyed much of that city. Seismographs record them. For 10 points, name this natural disaster.
This is the term for a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure, such as quartz. For 10 points, name this basic constituent of rocks.

This climate phenomenon features the periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. It weakens trade winds and disrupts weather across the Americas. For 10 points, name this phenomenon, whose Spanish name refers to the Christ Child.

This gas, emitted when fossil fuels are burned, is the main greenhouse gas driving recent climate change. It is also absorbed by plants during photosynthesis, and dissolves in the oceans to make them more acidic. Ice cores show its concentration over hundreds of thousands of years. For 10 points, name this gas with formula CO2.
This is the water-bearing layer of permeable rock or sediment that stores groundwater and can be tapped by wells. The Ogallala is a large American example. For 10 points, name this underground layer.

In 1909 a Croatian seismologist found that seismic waves speed up abruptly at about 30 to 50 kilometers beneath continents. This marks the base of the crust and the top of the mantle. For 10 points, name this discontinuity, abbreviated to its first four letters.

This geologic era, the "age of reptiles," includes the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods. It ended with an extinction 66 million years ago. For 10 points, name this era, between the Paleozoic and Cenozoic.

This is the term for the long-term pattern of weather in a region, as opposed to day-to-day conditions. It is usually defined by averaging temperature and precipitation over thirty years or more. The Koppen system classifies types of it. For 10 points, name this average of conditions, distinct from weather.

text: This scale rates the intensity of tornadoes by the damage they cause, from zero to five. It was developed in 1971 by a University of Chicago meteorologist and revised in 2007 to account for construction quality. An EF5 has winds over 200 miles per hour. For 10 points, name this scale named for its creator.

This limit, equal to about 1.4 solar masses, is the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf supported by electron degeneracy pressure. It was calculated in 1930 by an Indian-American astrophysicist on a voyage to England. Stars above it end as neutron stars or black holes. For 10 points, name this mass limit named for a Nobel laureate.

This diagram plots stellar luminosity against surface temperature or spectral type, revealing a main sequence, giants, and white dwarfs. It was developed independently by a Dane and an American in the early twentieth century. For 10 points, name this diagram named for two astronomers, abbreviated H-R.

This law, discovered by an American astronomer in 1929, states that galaxies recede from us at speeds proportional to their distances. It provided the first evidence for the expansion of the universe. For 10 points, name this law named for an astronomer who also has a space telescope named for him.

This is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Its radius is given by two times the gravitational constant times the mass divided by the speed of light squared. For 10 points, name this surface named for what you see happening at the horizon.
This is the closest star to Earth other than the Sun, about four light-years away. It is a red dwarf in the Alpha Centauri system. For 10 points, name this star whose name implies it is the nearest.

These pulsating radio sources were discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish. They are rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of radiation. For 10 points, name these objects, whose name combines "pulsating" and "star."

This radiation, discovered by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in 1965 as unexplained noise in a horn antenna, has a blackbody temperature of about 2.7 kelvin. It is the leftover glow from the early universe, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. For 10 points, name this radiation, abbreviated CMB.
This planet has the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, and a reddish color due to iron oxide. It has two moons, Phobos and Deimos. For 10 points, name this fourth planet from the Sun.

This is the term for a star's apparent shift in position as the Earth orbits the Sun. Friedrich Bessel first measured it for 61 Cygni in 1838. For 10 points, name this effect used to measure distances to nearby stars, and the source of the parsec.

This is the name of our galaxy, a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across containing hundreds of billions of stars. The Sun lies in the Orion Arm, roughly halfway out from the center. Its name comes from the pale band of stars visible across the night sky. For 10 points, name this galaxy.
This object, the largest planet's most famous storm, is an anticyclone that has persisted for centuries. It is large enough to engulf Earth. For 10 points, name this feature in Jupiter's atmosphere.

These are the stable points in a two-body orbital system, where a small object can remain in a fixed position relative to the two large masses. The James Webb Space Telescope orbits the second one. There are five of them in all. For 10 points, name these points named for a French-Italian mathematician.

This is the process powering the Sun, in which hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium and release energy. It requires temperatures of millions of kelvin in the core. For 10 points, name this nuclear process, whose reverse is fission.
This is the planet with the most prominent ring system, composed mostly of ice. It has a moon called Titan with a thick atmosphere. For 10 points, name this planet, the sixth from the Sun.

This is the term for a star that has exhausted hydrogen in its core and expanded, cooled, and brightened, such as Betelgeuse and Arcturus. The Sun will become one in about five billion years. For 10 points, name this stage that follows the main sequence, which can be red.

This Polish astronomer proposed in De revolutionibus orbium coelestium that the Sun, rather than Earth, is at the center of the planetary system. He published it in 1543. For 10 points, name this man.

This is the first rocky world in the solar system, closest to the Sun, with the most extreme temperature swings. A day on it lasts longer than its year in some senses. For 10 points, name this planet, smallest in the solar system.

This is the term for a large, rotating system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter held together by gravity. Edwin Hubble classified them as spiral, elliptical, and irregular. The Milky Way and Andromeda are examples. For 10 points, give this term for an island universe of billions of stars.

This is the type of supernova that results from the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf accreting matter from a companion. Because they have consistent peak luminosity, they serve as standard candles, which showed that the expansion of the universe is accelerating. For 10 points, name this type, labeled with a Roman numeral and a letter.

This is the term for the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere over the course of a year. The zodiac constellations lie along it, and it is inclined about 23.4 degrees to the celestial equator. Eclipses can occur only when the Moon crosses it. For 10 points, name this great circle.

This force holds planets in orbit around the Sun and keeps the Moon circling Earth. Newton explained it with a universal law in which it is proportional to the product of two masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. Einstein later described it as curvature of spacetime. For 10 points, name this fundamental force.

This astronomer used Tycho Brahe's careful observations of Mars to derive three laws of planetary motion. He found that planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus, sweep out equal areas in equal times, and obey a period-distance relation. He published them in Astronomia Nova and Harmonices Mundi. For 10 points, name this German astronomer.

This is the name of the invisible substance that makes up about 85 percent of the matter in the universe, inferred from galactic rotation curves studied by Vera Rubin. It does not emit or absorb light. For 10 points, name this substance.

This is the name for a ball of ice, dust, and rock whose gas and dust tails point away from the Sun as it nears it. The nucleus is often called a dirty snowball, and its coma forms as ices sublimate. Halley's is the most famous periodic one, returning about every 76 years. For 10 points, name this kind of small solar system body.

This dwarf planet was discovered by Clyde Tombaugh at Lowell Observatory in 1930 and was reclassified by the International Astronomical Union in 2006. It has a large moon named Charon, and New Horizons flew past it in 2015. A heart-shaped plain called Tombaugh Regio is on its surface. For 10 points, name this world.

This is the most volcanically active body in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes and lava lakes. Its surface is colored yellow and orange by sulfur compounds. Tidal heating from orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede drives its activity. For 10 points, name this innermost Galilean moon.

This is the type of eclipse in which the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, casting a shadow on part of the planet. A total one reveals the faint outer corona and lasts at most about seven and a half minutes. A path of totality sweeps across the surface. For 10 points, name this eclipse, as opposed to a lunar one.

This is the dwarf planet and largest object in the asteroid belt, visited by NASA's Dawn spacecraft in 2015. It was first discovered by Giuseppe Piazzi in 1801. For 10 points, name this world named for a Roman goddess of agriculture.
This is the term for an exploding massive star at the end of its life, which can briefly outshine a galaxy. The Crab Nebula is the remnant of one seen in 1054. For 10 points, name this event.

text: These pulsating stars have a period-luminosity relation discovered by Henrietta Swan Leavitt in 1912 from observations in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Hubble used them in Andromeda to show that it lies far outside the Milky Way. They are named for a star in the constellation Cepheus, and they serve as standard candles. For 10 points, name these variable stars.

This theorem states that the integral of a holomorphic function around a closed contour in a simply connected domain is zero. A consequence is an integral formula giving the value of a function inside a contour in terms of its values on the boundary. It is a foundation of complex analysis. For 10 points, name this theorem named for a French mathematician who also names a sequence criterion for convergence.

Kurt Godel proved two theorems with this word in their names, showing that any consistent formal system capable of arithmetic contains true statements that cannot be proved within it. They ended Hilbert's program of proving consistency of mathematics. For 10 points, give the word, referring to a quality of a system being unable to prove everything true.

This formula states that e raised to i times theta equals cosine theta plus i times sine theta. A special case with theta equal to pi gives an identity linking five fundamental constants: e to the i pi plus one equals zero. For 10 points, name this formula named for a Swiss mathematician.

This is the term for a group in which the operation is commutative, named for a Norwegian mathematician who died young. The integers under addition are an example. For 10 points, give this adjective, which also names a prize in mathematics.

This is the term for the set of all vectors that a linear transformation maps to zero. Its dimension is called the nullity, and the rank-nullity theorem relates it to the rank. For 10 points, name this subspace, also called the null space.

This conjecture, one of the Millennium Prize Problems, asks whether the nontrivial zeros of a certain complex function all have real part one half. It has implications for the distribution of primes. For 10 points, name this conjecture about the zeta function.

This theorem states that if a function is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on the open interval, there is a point where the derivative equals the average rate of change. For 10 points, name this theorem used to prove many results in calculus.

Euler solved this problem in 1735, finding that the sum of the reciprocals of the squares of the positive integers equals pi squared over six. It was posed by Pietro Mengoli and resisted attacks by the Bernoulli family. It is named for the Swiss city that was the hometown of Euler. For 10 points, name this problem.

This is the name for a number of the form a plus b i, whose conjugate is a minus b i, and whose magnitude is the square root of a squared plus b squared. For 10 points, name this extension of the real numbers.

In graph theory, this theorem says that the vertices of any planar map can be colored with at most four colors so that no adjacent regions share a color. It was first proved in 1976 by Appel and Haken using a computer. For 10 points, name this theorem about coloring maps.

This is the name of the method of finding roots of a function by iterating x minus f of x over f prime of x. It converges quadratically near simple roots. For 10 points, name this method named for an English physicist, also called the Newton-Raphson method.
This is the term for the number of ways to arrange n distinct objects in order, equal to n factorial. There are six of these of the letters A, B, and C. For 10 points, name this counting concept.

This is the type of matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else. Multiplying any compatible matrix by it leaves the matrix unchanged, so it plays the role that the number one plays for real numbers. Its determinant is one, and it is its own inverse. For 10 points, name this matrix.

This theorem states that a continuous function from a closed ball to itself must have a point where f of x equals x. It was proved by a Dutch mathematician and implies that stirring coffee leaves some point in place. For 10 points, name this fixed-point theorem.

This is the term for the distribution with a probability density function proportional to e to the negative x squared over two, with mean zero and variance one in its standard form. The central limit theorem says sample means approach it. For 10 points, name this bell-shaped distribution.
This is the term for a statement that is assumed to be true without proof, such as the parallel postulate in Euclid. For 10 points, give this term for a starting assumption in a mathematical system.

This function, defined as the integral from zero to infinity of t to the x minus one times e to the negative t, extends the factorial to complex numbers. For 10 points, name this function symbolized by a Greek capital letter.

This is the term for a set that can be put into one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers. The integers and rationals are examples, but Cantor's diagonal argument shows the reals are not. For 10 points, name this adjective for a set the same size as the naturals.

This is the name for the theorem that states that every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root. Gauss gave the first widely accepted proof. For 10 points, name this theorem of algebra.

This is the name for the series expansion of a function about zero, with coefficients given by derivatives at zero divided by factorials. The expansion of e to the x is one plus x plus x squared over two and so on. For 10 points, name this series named for a Scottish mathematician, a special case of Taylor series.

This is the term for the point where a graph crosses the vertical axis, found by setting x equal to zero. In the slope-intercept form of a line, y equals m x plus b, it is the constant b. For the parabola y equals x squared plus three, it equals three. For 10 points, name this feature of a graph.

This is the type of number that cannot be written as a ratio of two integers, such as the square root of two. The Pythagorean Hippasus is said to have proved their existence. For 10 points, name this class of real numbers.

This is the name of the constant, approximately 0.5772, defined as the limit of the harmonic sum minus the natural logarithm of n. It is named for two mathematicians, a Swiss and an Italian. For 10 points, name this constant, symbolized by a Greek gamma.

This is the type of statistical test that uses a distribution named for a British-born statistician writing as "Student" at the Guinness brewery. It is used for small samples. For 10 points, name this test.

This is the name for the line that divides a segment into two equal parts at a right angle. Every point on it is equidistant from the two endpoints of the segment. The three of them in a triangle meet at the circumcenter. For 10 points, name this line.
This is the measure of how much a curve bends, equal to the reciprocal of the radius of the osculating circle. A straight line has zero of it. For 10 points, name this geometric quantity.

This conjecture states that every simply connected, closed three-dimensional manifold is homeomorphic to the three-sphere. It was proved by Grigori Perelman using Ricci flow, following a program of Richard Hamilton. Perelman declined the Fields Medal and the Millennium Prize for it. For 10 points, name this conjecture, the first Millennium Prize Problem to be solved.

text: A Greek scholar who was head of the Library of Alexandria and also measured the circumference of the Earth devised this method for finding primes. One lists the integers from two up, then repeatedly crosses out all multiples of each surviving number. The numbers that remain are prime. For 10 points, name this ancient algorithm named for that scholar.

This function of a real number returns its distance from zero, so the value for negative three is three. Its graph is V-shaped with a corner at the origin. It is written with two vertical bars around the input. For 10 points, name this function that makes negatives positive.

This number, approximately 1.618, equals one plus the square root of five, all divided by two. The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approaches it. It is denoted by a Greek letter and appears in the pentagram and in Euclid's extreme and mean ratio. For 10 points, name this ratio.

This three-dimensional shape has volume four thirds pi r cubed and surface area four pi r squared. Archimedes was so proud of relating its volume to that of a circumscribed cylinder that it was reportedly shown on his tomb. Every point on its surface is the same distance from its center. For 10 points, name this round solid.

This class of problems consists of decision problems whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time. Whether it equals the class P of problems solvable in polynomial time is one of the Millennium Prize Problems. Stephen Cook and Leonid Levin proved that the satisfiability problem is complete for it. For 10 points, name this complexity class abbreviated with two letters.

This problem asks whether a program will finish running or loop forever for a given input. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can decide it for all program-input pairs. The proof uses a diagonalization argument. For 10 points, name this undecidable problem.

This graph traversal algorithm extends a shortest-path method by adding a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance to the goal, ordering nodes by the sum of cost so far and that estimate. It is optimal if the heuristic never overestimates. It was developed at the Stanford Research Institute for the robot Shakey. For 10 points, name this pathfinding algorithm commonly used in video games, whose name is a letter followed by a punctuation symbol.

This sorting algorithm repeatedly divides the list in half, sorts each half recursively, and then combines them in order. It is stable and always runs in n log n time, but needs extra memory. John von Neumann described it in 1945. For 10 points, name this divide-and-conquer sort.

This is the term for a program that translates human-readable source code into machine code for execution, as opposed to an interpreter. For 10 points, name this type of program that includes GCC and Clang.

This is the term for a self-balancing binary search tree named for two Soviet mathematicians, in which the heights of the two subtrees of any node differ by at most one. For 10 points, name this tree, the first self-balancing binary search tree, with names of its inventors.

This is the 1976 public-key scheme, named for two Stanford researchers, that allows two parties to establish a shared secret over a public channel using modular exponentiation. Its security rests on the discrete logarithm problem. For 10 points, name this key exchange.

This is the architecture of most modern computers, described in 1945, where program instructions and data are stored in the same memory. It is named for a Hungarian-American mathematician. For 10 points, name this architecture.

This is the language used for most programming on Apple's iOS devices after 2014, replacing Objective-C. Its name is also a fast bird. For 10 points, name this language created by Chris Lattner at Apple.

This is the term for the principle that a database transaction is all or nothing, one of the four ACID properties. The others are consistency, isolation, and durability. For 10 points, name this property.

This 1936 mathematical model uses lambda abstraction and function application to express computation. It was developed by Alonzo Church and underlies functional programming languages like Lisp and Haskell. For 10 points, name this formal system.

This is the concept in operating systems of a small unit of execution within a process that shares memory with other such units. Using several allows a program to do tasks concurrently. For 10 points, name this unit.

This is the term for unwanted messages sent in bulk by email, usually advertising or scams. Filters use machine learning to detect it, and laws regulate it. Its name comes from a canned meat in a Monty Python sketch. For 10 points, name this nuisance in inboxes.

This protocol, created at Netscape in the 1990s and later standardized as TLS, encrypts traffic between a web browser and a server. The padlock icon in a browser indicates it. For 10 points, name this protocol abbreviated SSL.

This self-balancing tree data structure keeps data sorted and allows searches, insertions, and deletions in logarithmic time, with each node holding many keys and children. Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight invented it at Boeing in 1971. Databases and file systems use it to minimize disk reads. For 10 points, name this tree, whose name suggests letters rather than a number of branches.

This is the term for a technique where a function's results for given inputs are stored to avoid recomputation, speeding up the recursive Fibonacci algorithm. It is related to dynamic programming. For 10 points, name this technique.

This is the logic gate that outputs true only if both of its inputs are true. Its truth table has a single row with output one, when both inputs are one. In circuit diagrams it is drawn with a flat input side and a rounded output side. For 10 points, name this basic gate, often paired with OR and NOT.

This is the neural network type that uses layers of filters sliding over inputs and is widely used for image recognition. AlexNet won the ImageNet competition in 2012 using one. For 10 points, name this kind of network, abbreviated CNN.

This is the 1950 test proposed by Alan Turing in which a human judge converses with a machine and a human and tries to tell which is which. For 10 points, give the other name for the "imitation game."

This is the term for an attack in which malicious SQL code is inserted into a form field to manipulate a database query. Parameterized queries prevent it. For 10 points, name this attack, abbreviated with a three-letter language name and a word for putting something in.

This is the term for a unit of digital information equal to 1,024 bytes in some conventions, or 1,000 in SI. The next larger unit is the megabyte. For 10 points, name this unit, prefixed by a metric word for thousand.

This is the file format that is a lossy image compression standard named for the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Digital cameras commonly save photos in it. For 10 points, give this format's name, which also has a three-letter extension.

This Finnish software engineer released the first version of a free Unix-like operating system kernel in 1991 as a hobby, and later created a distributed version control system. For 10 points, name this person, whose kernel runs on Android phones and most web servers.
